Sometimes, people entered the room, but her impaired vision prevented her from identifying them. The nanomaterial left her short-sighted, only able to make out blurry shapes and colors. Occasionally, someone would inspect her like a piece of art, walking close to the cage without acknowledging her humanity. They behaved as if it were completely normal to have a glistening black shiny latex woman as an ornament in the living room.
Keiko’s mind raced with memories of her past. She thought of the skills she had honed, the victories she had achieved. Bound and helpless, she clung to those memories. She recalled the katana heist, the thrill of outsmarting Hayashi, and the satisfaction of seeing justice done. She thought of the people she had helped, the lives she had touched through her heists.
In her moments of silence, she planned. She studied the cage, the routines, the people who came and went. She knew she couldn’t escape with brute force, but there had to be a way. The nanomaterial was powerful, but it couldn’t be flawless. She observed, waited, and endured, her mind constantly working on a plan.
But despite her efforts, no progress was made. The days dragged on, with Keiko standing in place, barely able to move. Her mind was idle, her body cramped, and her situation hopeless. Nothing happened, and she was left with nothing but her thoughts and the endless torment of her captivity.
A week passed, each day a repeat of the same humiliating routine. Keiko endured the degrading feeding and littering rituals, the forced standing, and the painful punishments from the suit whenever she resisted. She tried to keep her spirit strong, but the constant degradation and torment wore her down.
On the seventh day, Hartmann approached her cage, his expression cold and distant. He pulled out his phone, and once again, the gag retracted. Keiko’s mouth, plugged and stretched for so long, struggled to form words. Her throat was dry, and when she spoke, her voice came out as a hoarse whisper.
“Who are you? Who sent you? What were you after?” Hartmann asked, his tone mocking. He had placed the diadem on her himself. He already knew the answers. This wasn’t about gaining information—it was about breaking her down, stripping away her defiance piece by piece.
Keiko thought about hurling insults again, but the memory of the punishment made her shudder. Instead, she remained silent, her eyes burning with defiance behind the thin layer of black material covering them.
Hartmann’s smile widened with cruel satisfaction. “Ah, the silent treatment? Very well.” He pressed a button on his phone, and the gag reappeared in Keiko’s mouth. She braced herself for what would follow.
The pain hit her with the same intensity as before, burning through her body like fire. She convulsed, her muscles seizing up against the tight grip of the nanomaterial. Every second dragged on in agony, each moment more unbearable than the last.
Finally, the pain stopped, and Keiko was left alone in her cage. The same cycle resumed: boredom, humiliation, and unrelenting pain. Keiko clung to memories of her past victories, trying to draw strength from the knowledge that she had beaten impossible odds before.
Another week passed, and Keiko felt her resolve crumbling. The isolation, the routine, and the endless pain were breaking her down. She realized that Hartmann had no limits—he would continue this forever if it meant watching her spirit break completely. That night, she lay curled in the too-small cage, unable to stretch because touching the cage bars would mean punishment. She was crying, but the nanomaterial absorbed her tears, erasing even the smallest sign of her suffering.
Keiko understood now. The only thing that would make any difference to Hartmann was her total compliance. The realization crushed the last bit of her defiance. She decided that next time he asked, she would answer him.
When Hartmann returned a week later, he found her standing, head bowed, her spirit dulled. He activated the phone, and the gag retracted.
“Who are you? Who sent you? What were you after?” His voice was cold, the mocking tone still present.
Keiko’s voice was soft and broken. “My name is Keiko Toda. No one sent me. I was after the Diadem of Lyria.”
Hartmann smiled, satisfied. “Good. That wasn’t so hard, was it?”
Even after she gave him what he wanted, Hartmann reactivated the gag and left her as before—caged and ignored. Her cooperation had spared her punishment, but it hadn’t changed anything. The torment continued, with no end in sight.
In her solitude, Keiko faced the full weight of her hopelessness. She had nothing left to offer Hartmann, nothing to bargain for her freedom. And even if she had, she knew he would never trade with her. He was a sadist who derived pleasure from her suffering. Her fate was sealed.
Hartmann wanted to see her broken, and he had succeeded. She remembered him telling the story of Lyria, the priestess who wore the same diadem now sitting on her own head. It was clear what her future would be. No one would rescue her. Nobody would oppose someone so rich, nobody would come to rescue her. Least of all Hartmann himself, who enjoyed her despair.
Keiko’s spirit was gone. She felt hollow, her strength and defiance crushed. She had done everything Hartmann asked, but it hadn’t saved her from the cruel monotony of her existence. There was no hope left, no resistance. Keiko was no longer the Shadow Siren. She wasn’t even Keiko anymore. She was whatever Hartmann wanted her to be, and she would do whatever he ordered her to do.
Plaything# Another week passed, and the humiliation and isolation were even harder to bear. Keiko had revealed everything, but nothing changed. The routine stayed the same: tasteless meals, public degradation, and endless silence.
When Hartmann appeared again, he tapped his phone, and the sleek nanomaterial changed. It uncovered her face, forming an open hood, and released her arms, though her hands were now trapped in featureless ball mittens, forcing them into fists. A tight corset shaped her body, pushing her into a presentation pose that felt obscene. Heels formed around her feet, adding to her discomfort.
Hartmann smiled, his eyes gleaming with cruel satisfaction. “You can move around the villa now,” he said. “You won’t speak unless spoken to, and you’ll answer respectfully and truthfully. You’ll answer ‘Sir’ or ‘Ma’am.’”
He continued, “When you kneel, the suit will lock your feet to your thighs, freeing your hands. Once you make fists again, the mittens will return, and you’ll be able to stand. Feeding, relieving yourself, and sleeping will still happen in the cage. No sitting or lying down anywhere else. You may lie down after dark in your cage, and only then.”
Hartmann’s eyes gleamed with sadistic pleasure. “If you try to escape or communicate with anyone outside, you’ll go back to the cage, no second chances.”
He laughed a supervillain’s laugh. Then he casually added, “Ah, and finally, you will obey any order from anyone, without hesitation or questioning. You will be a public plaything.”
Keiko knew Hartmann would take pleasure in enforcing these rules. She decided she had no choice but to follow them. Her cage opened, and she stepped out, though she hardly felt free. The corset forced her into an unnatural posture, and the height of the heels made every step a challenge.
Hartmann left her standing in the luxurious living room. For the first time, she could see the luxury that surrounded her. She took a tentative step, struggling with the heels. The corset restricted her movements, but she was thankful for the chance to move at all. She wandered through the villa, its vastness mocking her situation.
The rooms were grand, filled with art and expensive furniture. She found the library, the dining room, and sitting rooms, all empty. Every step reminded her of the rules Hartmann had set. The weight of the suit and the fear of punishment made her cautious.
Turning a corner, Keiko saw her reflection in a full-length mirror. She froze, staring at herself. Her entire body was encased in the shiny, glistening black material, covering her from neck to toe while leaving only her face visible. The material clung to her form, highlighting every curve and muscle, accentuating her body in a way that felt both revealing and confining.
The corset pulled her waist tight, pushing her breasts up in a way that felt provocative. It forced her into an exaggerated hourglass shape, making her movements stiff and controlled. The high heels extended her legs, putting her on tiptoe, exaggerating her posture and making her body feel like it was on display. Her nipples were clearly visible through the thin material, completing the dehumanizing effect.
On her head, the Diadem of Lyria glittered mockingly. The very artifact she had tried to steal now marked her as a slave, just like the priestess of legend. The beauty of the diadem contrasted sharply with her degradation, a cruel reminder of her lost freedom. Keiko’s reflection was that of a living statue, a symbol of servitude, adorned with a crown that mockingly symbolized her total submission and loss of identity.
Testing the limits of her new freedom, Keiko knelt in a secluded corner. As promised, the suit locked her feet to her thighs and freed her hands, now covered in sleek black gloves. She flexed her fingers, enjoying the brief moment of freedom before forming fists again. The mittens reappeared, and her legs unlocked, allowing her to stand.
Feeding time was as degrading as ever, and her bodily functions were still a public spectacle. The maid approached with cold authority. “Back into your cage, now,” she commanded sharply.
Keiko obeyed, keeping her head down as she returned to the cage. The maid pushed the litter box inside. “Assume the position,” she ordered.
Keiko complied, crouching down, legs spread wide, despite the presence of visitors in the room. She was acutely aware of the impending punishment that any resistance would carry. The visitors watched with detached interest, their eyes following her every move.
The suit controlled her body, emptying her waste without her having any control. The sensation was humiliating, a constant reminder of her helplessness. The unknown visitors stood by, looking interested in the process, commenting among themselves as if Keiko were an object or an animal on display.
“Fascinating how the suit handles everything,” one of them remarked.
“Indeed,” another replied. “Quite efficient, isn’t it?”
Keiko barely registered the humiliation anymore. She was completely broken, her spirit shattered. Their comments meant nothing to her. Her identity as Keiko, the Shadow Siren, was gone.
When the suit finished, the maid gave another order. “Take the litterbox to the trash.”
Keiko responded automatically, “Yes, Ma’am.” She picked up the litterbox, her movements precise and obedient, and carried it to the trash bin. She performed the task mechanically, her fear of punishment driving her every action.
The humiliation and degradation were now part of her daily life, a constant reminder of her broken state. She no longer felt shame or resistance. She was just a tool, a thing for others to use. Her spirit, once so strong, had been crushed under the weight of her captivity.
At night, she returned to her cage. The unyielding corset made it even more cramped, but she was allowed to lie down. It was the only relief she had, though even then, the tightness of the suit never let her forget her situation. Keiko’s former life and identity were gone, replaced by a hollow shell, a living symbol of servitude.
The maid took even more advantage of Keiko, ordering her to perform menial tasks throughout the day. Keiko had no choice but to obey. One afternoon, the maid commanded her to kneel in a corner of the kitchen, facing the wall of course. As she knelt, the suit shifted, locking her legs to her thighs and freeing her hands. The maid handed her a drawer full of heavily tarnished silverware.
“Polish all of this until it shines,” the maid ordered coldly. “Be quick, no pauses.”
Keiko’s hands shook as she picked up the first piece. She opened her mouth to ask how long this would take, but the moment she spoke, a sharp electric shock jolted through her. She wasn’t allowed to speak unless spoken to. She cried out, but that brought another zap, stronger this time. No sounds either. She clenched her teeth, trying to suppress her cries, but every gasp earned her more pain. The maid stood by, watching with a twisted smile.
Tears rolled down Keiko’s cheeks as she focused on the task, her hands scrubbing at the tarnished silver with frantic energy. Her shoulders burned from the repetitive motions, but she couldn’t stop. Pausing, even for a second, brought another surge of agony that left her breathless.
Every command and every shock deepened her sense of helplessness. She could feel the maid taking pleasure in the power she held, enjoying every bit of Keiko’s suffering. The Shadow Siren—once proud, skilled, and strong—was now reduced to a tool for others’ amusement.
Hours passed, each one dragging on longer than the last, and Keiko’s despair grew heavier. Every shock eroded her spirit a little more, and the hopelessness in her mind deepened. She felt herself slipping further away, her identity dissolving under the constant weight of obedience. The maid’s orders echoed in her head, each word a reminder of her complete powerlessness.
Keiko knew she was trapped. Her life had become a series of humiliations and punishments, and she had nothing left. The fight had been beaten out of her, her defiance long gone. She was no longer a person but a thing to be used and discarded at the whim of her captors. In the darkest parts of her mind, she began to accept this, her dreams of rebellion and justice crumbling into dust.
Broken# As Keiko finished polishing the last piece of silverware, the butler appeared, his presence looming over her. He ordered her to make fists, and the mittens reformed around her hands. Her legs unlocked, and she was told to get up and move to the butler’s quarters, where she would wait, kneeling in front of the bed.
“Yes, Sir,” Keiko replied, her voice flat, emotionless.
She walked toward the butler’s quarters, dread weighing down each step. She had a good idea of what was coming, but disobedience was not an option. When she reached the room, she knelt before the bed, and the suit shifted again, locking her legs into position. She was immobilized, left with nothing to do but wait.
As Keiko knelt there, she felt the weight of the Diadem of Lyria on her head, a constant reminder of her dual role: a trophy and a slave. It was both a symbol of her worth and the mark of her subjugation. Its presence, heavy on her skull, pushed her further into submission, an emblem of everything she had lost.
Eventually, the butler, whose name she did not even know, appeared and sat down on the bed in front of her. “Open my pants with your mouth and service me,” he ordered, his voice devoid of emotion.
Keiko’s stomach churned with disgust, but fear of punishment drove her to obedience. She leaned forward, using her mouth to unfasten his pants, her actions mechanical and detached. Keiko, trained by the phallic feeder and worn down by weeks of captivity, complied with his orders, performing as he demanded. She had no problem, taking him in fully, her feeder was by far more unrelenting and demanding than this man. She performed the degrading act, her mind numb to the humiliation, focusing only on completing the task to avoid further pain, using her tongue and following his orders as he directed her. With every movement, she felt the weight of the diadem on her head moving, reminding of her status and mocking her. Eventually, he would use his hands, grab her encased head, and hold her, relentlessly fucking her mouth until he came.
When he was done, he ordered her to clean up. “Yes, Sir,” she whispered, complying with his demands. Afterward, he told her to make fists again, the mittens reformed, locking her hands. Her legs were freed, and he sent her back to her cage.
Keiko stood up, feeling dirty and violated, and returned to her cage. The same routine awaited her: feeding from the phallic rod, enduring the tasteless mush, and squatting before the litter box as the suit managed her bodily functions. All of it felt meaningless now—just another part of her day.
That night, she was allowed to lie down in her cage. The door was left open, but Keiko didn’t dare move. She knew better than to test the boundaries. The small relief of being able to lie down was overshadowed by the knowledge that tomorrow would bring more of the same.
As she lay there, her thoughts were heavy with despair. She had been broken. Hartmann’s cruelty, along with the constant commands of the maid and butler, had crushed her spirit. She was no longer the Shadow Siren, or even Keiko. She was a tool for others to use, her will shattered.
Each day blurred into the next, a loop of obedience and humiliation. Keiko’s compliance became automatic, her actions driven by fear of punishment rather than any sense of self. She no longer thought of escape or rebellion—those ideas had faded along with her sense of identity. Even Hartmann, who had once been the center of her hate and resistance, became a distant figure, indifferent to her existence unless he wanted to show off his control.
When Keiko searched her mind for some spark of resistance, she found nothing. The inner sanctuary where she once drew strength was gone, unreachable. Her past life was fading away, leaving her a hollow shell, defined by her new reality as an object of service and humiliation. She was no longer upset by it—it was simply the way things were. Obedience kept the pain at bay, and that was all that mattered now.
Keiko understood that her fate had been sealed from the moment the nanomaterial touched her skin. She never had a chance. Hartmann had planned everything, and she had been naïve to think she could have control over her destiny. Now, he ruled over her life, like an unreachable god, and she belonged to him and his servants.
Her days settled into an unchanging pattern. She worked as ordered, cleaned, and carried out the maid’s endless commands. She knelt and serviced the butler when called upon, her mind empty, her body compliant. The constant humiliation and degradation no longer cut as deep; they had simply become the fabric of her existence.
Keiko’s inner world became blank, her past washed away by relentless conditioning. She lived in the present, performing tasks without thought or emotion. She was an object, stripped of agency, purpose, and hope. In rare moments of reflection, she understood that this was her life now. She existed to serve, to endure, and to obey.
Hartmann’s design had succeeded. She was no longer a person but a possession, her will extinguished, her identity dissolved. She moved through her days as if in a trance, responding only to the commands of those who controlled her. And as the weeks turned into months, Keiko accepted her fate fully. Her spirit was gone, and she was nothing more than a plaything, living only to please her captors.
Entertainment# Keiko’s transformation into a silent, obedient ornament was complete. She moved through Hartmann’s villa with practiced ease, her every action graceful and automatic. Each command was met with a smile and a polite curtsy, just as she had been trained.
Hartmann felt secure in her obedience, proudly displaying her as his trophy. For special occasions, the nanomaterial molded into a striking black outfit that emphasized her role. A tight corset cinched her waist, pushing her breasts up provocatively, while the material flared into an ornate skirt, resembling luxurious fabric. Her legs were wrapped in high-heeled boots that forced her into an elegant posture. A half-hood covered her head, leaving only her eyes and mouth visible. Her hands were free, allowing her to serve the guests more efficiently. Looking at her, there was no mistaking her role—she was a living symbol of submission.
The guests at Hartmann’s parties were as cruel as he was. They took delight in commanding her, knowing that she had no choice but to obey. Keiko walked among them, serving drinks and offering smiles that never reached her eyes. Each interaction was a fresh humiliation, a reminder of her complete and utter defeat.
Sometimes Hartmann would order her to smile, ensuring her expression matched the perfect, polished demeanor he demanded. Other times, he had her wear the Diadem of Lyria, showing it off to guests, emphasizing her servitude. And always, he made sure she was available for their pleasure. The guests took advantage of her, ordering her around with no room for refusal. The suit and her training made sure she complied with every request.
She was only to speak when spoken to, always polite, always respectful. The guests reveled in her compliance, each interaction stripping away more of her humanity. Keiko’s existence had become a constant cycle of enforced obedience, her role as a living trophy solidified.
As Keiko moved among the guests, her actions were smooth and well-practiced. She carried trays of canapés and drinks, keeping her gaze down. When addressed, she responded with a soft “Yes, Sir” or “Yes, Ma’am,” her voice devoid of emotion. The guests treated her as an object, a public plaything.
“What’s your story, girl?” one guest asked, a cruel curiosity flickering in his eyes.
Keiko recited what she had been taught. “My name was Keiko Toda. I was caught trying to steal from Mr. Hartmann, and I have been taught to serve. I am grateful for the lessons he has given me.”
“And what do you offer?” another guest asked with a lecherous tone.
“I offer drinks, entertainment, and pleasure,” Keiko replied without hesitation. “I am here for your enjoyment.”
Throughout the night, Keiko was used in various ways. Some guests made her kneel and service them, while others ordered her to perform degrading tasks for their amusement. One particularly cruel guest enjoyed making her repeat her story, delighting in the way her voice cracked slightly with each telling.
“Such a lovely addition to the party,” he sneered. “A reminder of what happens when you cross Viktor Hartmann.”
Occasionally, guests would compliment Hartmann on his ’trophy.’ In response, Keiko would say, “I am thankful to Mr. Hartmann for teaching me these valuable lessons. I am honored to serve.”
In the center of the room stood her cage, a clear symbol of her captivity. Keiko’s eyes were constantly drawn to it, the bars a stark reminder of her imprisonment. Some guests would point at it, laughing about her time spent confined within its black steel.
Hartmann watched with satisfaction as Keiko moved through the crowd, a living testament to his power and control. He knew she was completely broken, her spirit extinguished, and her obedience absolute. She was a hollow shell, an obedient servant, her past and identity erased by the relentless conditioning. She was Hartmann’s trophy, his obedient servant, and she would remain so until he decided otherwise.
Keiko knew that, like Lyria, she would eventually be sold once Hartmann grew tired of her. It was a fate she had already accepted. She understood that she was nothing more than an object to be traded, her value measured by her submission. The story of the diadem had come full circle—just as Lyria was passed from master to master, so too would Keiko be.
And so she served, silent and obedient, her cage always in view. It stood as a constant reminder of what she had become, her fate sealed by the very thing she had once sought to steal—the Diadem of Lyria.

title: Chapter 10: Sonia packs and flies to Shanghai
content:
Sonia packs and flies to Shanghai# Checking into GAIA, Sonia surveyed her surroundings. She quickly identified a large number of Changed individuals, distinguished by their unique style of dress and behavior. “Let’s do some science,” she thought to herself, deciding to stay in the lobby for a bit to count, while Anna continued up to her office. “Changed versus Unchanged, let’s see the ratio.” Fifteen minutes later, she had her numbers: approximately 15 percent of all personnel, regardless of gender, had been Changed. She also overheard conversations about many people calling in sick, indicating the virus had infiltrated widely, altering people she once knew and imprinting itself on their bodies and minds. She understood she couldn’t trust those unaffected by the virus; their turn would come soon. For now, she had to find a way to fight the virus and find answers on her own, leveraging her own immunity.
Encumbered by the stupid Yoyah Sheengzoh and higher-than-comfortable heels, Sonia shuffled into her small above-ground office. She had to unbutton her blouse’s cuffs partly to be able to rid herself of the gloves, which was a nuisance, but gloved she could hardly type, and absolutely not use her trackpad. Finally, she was able to immerse herself in research. She collected reports, statistical data on infection rates, spread, and R-values, and built a timeline to pinpoint the origin of the infection. She noticed a curious parallel development between the infection and the “Maylee Shufoo” chain of stores. “Where the virus goes, the boutiques show up shortly after,” she noted. “Maybe that will let me put a face to the opposition. Unlike viruses, shops tend to have names attached to them. I’ll find out who owns these things.”
Corporate financial structures are different from genome data, but Sonia was deeply motivated. She checked LinkedIn and found few clues, except for Celine Durmont, listed as a boutique regional manager with skills in “Corporate Restructuring” and “Asset Protection,” and links to the consulting firm “Drexel and Saigne LLC.” The Geneva Chamber of Commerce registrations for Maylee Shufoo boutiques in Geneva led her to Veridis Quo, a holding listing one Maximilian Grothe, but that was a dead end. Maximilian Grothe had no findable public records, connections, or personal details.
“Okay, I have found some things, but I am truly out of my depth here,” she admitted to herself. “I need professional help. Very professional help.” In her mind, she went through a list of people that might be better suited than herself in trying to solve that. She decided to call Mara Delacroix, a high-powered independent corporate lawyer that GAIA usually worked with. Mara had handled contracts for GAIA concerning the acquisition of genome data and research contracts, and worked on legal policies for handling medical and other sensitive personal data. She wasn’t exactly a friend, Sonia wondered if “Mara, the Merciless” had any friends at all, but if anybody would get her results it would be her.
Since she was on a legal consulting contract with GAIA, getting Mara’s help was straightforward. They met for lunch at a small eatery around the corner from GAIA. That meant Sonia had to deal with the nuisance of her gloves and too many buttons again, twice, unless she wanted to incur the wrath of any Changed that saw her. Mara, a small, almost waifish figure, and visibly Unchanged, showed up dressed in a sharp business suit with almost no jewelry. She was obviously in a hurry. “Sonia, sorry for being late,” Mara apologized. “But I managed to squeeze you in for a quick lunch; I’ve been nearby,” she explained. “Thanks for coming, Mara.” They ordered sandwiches, some fruit juice, and a hot cocoa for Sonia.
“No coffee?” Mara inquired. “Have you ever met Anna?” Sonia replied, prompting a smile from Mara. “I don’t know what exactly she does to her stuff, but if you’ve ever had that, you’re a lost cause for coffee from places like this.”
Sonia explained her problem in a careful, non-specific way. “There is this new chain of shops that have been popping up all around Geneva. I… GAIA… we have reason to research them and find out the true owner of this chain. You may have seen them, Chinese-themed, Maylee Shufoo,” she began. “Oh, right,” Mara answered. “The Stepford wives/bondage shop crossover chain? Why would a genome research institute…” Sonia smiled thinly. “Right,” Mara stopped herself. “I don’t actually need an explanation. I’ll call you when I have found something. Anyway, this chain is weird, have you had a look…” Only then did Mara realize that Sonia was also wearing some Maylee Shufoo. “Wait. Why are you wearing their stuff? This is totally not your style. I mean, you can dress any way you want, but I would have never pegged you for… Sorry.” Mara caught herself.
“It’s fine. And you’re right. It is not my style,” Sonia responded. “But there’s a strange connection between Maylee Shufoo and a specific viral infection that I, I mean GAIA, needs to investigate.” Sonia paused, reflecting. “Maylee Shufoo is quite popular, and apparently, I need to fit in, being a field researcher and all.” It was a flimsy excuse, but it seemed sufficient for Mara, who was already mentally preparing for her next meeting.
Involving Mara turned out to be one of Sonia’s better decisions. Within just a day, Mara efficiently navigated what had seemed a daunting task to Sonia. The next morning, Sonia found a wealth of legal documents in her inbox: scans of corporate registrations, shell companies, annual and quarterly reports—all the essentials. The trails of evidence from Drexel and Saigne LLC and Veridis Quo Holdings pointed to a network of overseas ownership structures that included another boutique chain, 迷人的景象 or “Mirende Ginciao,” which Sonia automatically translated to “A Captivating Sight.” Known colloquially in the US market as “Mirren’s,” the chain also had a few outlets in some European regions and offered products very similar to Maylee Shufoo. The intricate corporate web pointed back to Shanghai, aligning with the Chinese theme of both chains.
Sonia had previously visited Shanghai on field trips and had friends and contacts there. Armed with the information from Mara, she sent out several emails seeking further details. The responses were mostly fruitless: Zhou Wei, a journalist she knew, could provide no additional information and asked more questions than she was prepared to answer. Wang Jie, a tech entrepreneur, explored his local tech and network scenes, but his connections to the biosciences were too weak to be of any use in this context.
Ultimately, it was Jiang Han, known as “The Broker,” who had the information she needed, provided Sonia didn’t inquire about how it was obtained. “It’s strange. All leads point to Shanghai, and now to a single person. It’s almost like a cliché Bond villain scenario,” she mused as she sifted through the dossier, a collection of PDFs on her workstation.
Dr. Mingyu Cheng, an American-born Chinese man who had made his fortune in biotech—Sonia’s own field—founded Cheng Biotech Industries (CBI) in ‘96, aiming to revolutionize treatments for neurological disorders. Sonia was well aware of the company, and suddenly the virus seemed like a blatantly obvious scheme. “Treatment of neurological disorders, my ass,” she scoffed, her laugh hollow. Cheng’s profile and CBI’s activities fit the profile perfectly. Cheng himself was known as a recluse, residing in a hypermodern villa hidden within a park-sized lot in Shanghai’s Xuhui district. “There couldn’t possibly be a more supervillain-esque person matching this outrageous plot,” she thought. “He’s moved back to his ancestral homeland from New York, built himself a fortress among the wealthy, and he’s famously conservative, a control freak difficult to collaborate with if this documentation is even remotely accurate. I need to go to Shanghai to find out more, that much is clear.”
Clara Dumont at her desk at GAIA.
Sonia needed a way to get to Shanghai, and the path led through Clara Dumont, her skip-level manager and the Director of Genetic Research at GAIA. Clara oversaw all viral genome research teams, including the one that Sonia belonged to. Sonia planned to frame her excursion as a routine field trip to collect samples, officially to pinpoint Patient Zero for LASS-VASH-2024. Since the findings about the virus hadn’t been released yet, it was still classified as harmless but intriguing. With Anna being Changed, Sonia wasn’t sure if Anna retained any interest in escalating the situation. Nonetheless, Sonia believed that securing approval for a standard field trip should be straightforward. She drafted the proposal, sent it off, and prepared to discuss it during her one-on-one meeting with Clara later that day.
As Sonia entered Clara’s office, she was immediately struck by the Change in her manager. Clara, too, was among the Changed, something Sonia hadn’t anticipated despite knowing the significant number of Changed within GAIA. Clara’s appearance was markedly different: her figure suggested the use of shapewear, and she wore the uniform of the Changed. In her case, an impractically narrow gray skirt, a Victorian-inspired blouse that buttoned at the back, a hijab, and even indoors, light blue satin gloves.
Sonia, unsure how to interpret this new version of Clara, proceeded cautiously. The old Clara had been a figure of authority and respect; this Changed Clara was an enigma, potentially even an adversary. Yet, Sonia needed her approval for the mission to Shanghai. She presented her case with calculated normalcy.
“Clara,” Sonia started, maintaining her composure, “I’d like to conduct a field trip similar to our recent work in Shenzhen, to collect virus samples and possibly pinpoint Patient Zero.”
Clara listened intently, her response was unexpectedly supportive and devoid of the hesitation Sonia had braced for. “Of course, Sonia. Your initiative aligns perfectly with our objectives. Gathering more data on LASS-VASH-2024 is crucial, and I fully support your fieldwork in Shanghai.”
Sonia was taken aback by Clara’s quick endorsement. It wasn’t just the ease of the approval but the implicit trust Clara seemed to place in the venture. Sonia had expected some resistance or at least scrutiny, considering the risks, but Clara either didn’t connect her own transformation with the virus or chose to ignore it.
Instead, Clara’s response seemed to reflect a deep-seated belief in the benefits of the virus, a conviction that appeared to unite those who had been Changed. This realization made Sonia reflect on the broader implications as she left Clara’s office, approval in hand. The Changed, including Clara and previously Anna, demonstrated an uncanny level of cooperation and positivity towards the virus and its consequences, a phenomenon Sonia contemplated deeply as she prepared for her trip.
Sonia was more than a bit paranoid by now: with a mind-altering virus at play, she trusted nothing and no one, not even her own judgment. Why were the Changed so uniformly supportive of actions that sought to investigate or potentially undermine the virus? Was it a side effect of the conditioning, a deeply ingrained trust in the virus’s purpose? Or was it something more—a strategic compliance, fully aware that any efforts to understand the virus might inadvertently lead to its further spread?
With Clara’s approval secured, Sonia shifted her focus to preparing for her journey. She confirmed that her work visa for Shenzhen was still valid, as were her additional documentation and permits needed as a field researcher working with biohazards. She had currency, and her SIM card was still active in her Chinese phone. She resolved not to use her “western” phone with any Chinese applications. She viewed her trip to Shanghai as an opportunity to uncover the truth about the virus and its origins, and to trace its connections to Dr. Mingyu Chen. She wanted to better understand the role of the boutique chains that seemed to flourish in the wake of the epidemic.
Having booked her flights, Sonia decided to visit the local Maylee Shufoo near her home. Now that she knew it was definitively connected to the virus, she was able to look at it differently and might be able to gain more insights. What she discovered was that the clothing had become even more restrictive. The new offerings at Maylee Shufoo included corsets, which hadn’t been there before, and a new item called 高抱佑护, “Gowbao Yoohoo” or “Embrace and Protect.” This variant of the well-known Victorian blouses she was already familiar with featured a higher neck that was internally reinforced with a leather collar, resembling a neck corset. It was completely impractical and very restrictive, and when completely closed would lock the wearers head in a specific position, straight upright, gaze forward and slightly downward, a unique combination of regal posture with submissive head position. It buttoned at the back, and the buttons on the arms ran from the elbow to the wrist on the outside of each arm. Opening or closing it involved dealing with dozens of minuscule buttons in unreachable locations, impossible to work with gloves on. Clearly, it was designed so that someone else had to help put it on or take it off.
Sonia thought deeply about the name, trying to decipher its meaning. It suggested “high embrace” or “to hold closely,” and “to protect,” or “bless and protect.” Together, these conveyed a sense of care and security. Yet, the garment itself told a different story—it was all about constraint and control.
The “high embrace” implied a suffocating closeness, leaving no room for movement or independence. The notion of protection morphed into a form of guardianship that demanded submission. The garment, with its tight neck and unremovable embrace, embodied the virus’s goal: to reshape people into obedient figures from the past, under the guise of care and protection.
And with each iteration, the fashions of “Beautiful Restraint” became more restrictive, making their wearer more dependent and less autonomous. The link between the virus and these garments showed how society was changing. The virus and the boutiques spread their ideology of control and submission. The world was becoming a place where old-fashioned looks hid a reality of control.
As she boarded her plane, Sonia knew: she had to act fast to find a way to fight back against the virus.

title: Chapter 11: Anna and Julien
Chapter 12: Lakeside Proposal
content:
Lakeside Proposal# Saturday at the Lakeside Café was like a dance for Anna and Julien, each step affirming their roles. Julien, ever the gentleman, offered his arm to Anna as they approached the café, his attentiveness making her feel cherished and protected.
Navigating the café in her “dress to impress” outfit required Julien’s assistance. Anna wore a stunning S-line corset with integrated shoulder braces and a Gowbao Yoohoo blouse. The corset cinched her waist, emphasizing her figure, while the blouse featured a high, reinforced collar that kept her head held high and her gaze demurely lowered.
As they found a spot to sit, Julien carefully guided Anna to her chair. The layered underskirt and tight corset made sitting a calculated act. Julien had to pull the chair out far enough for Anna to back into it gracefully, aligning herself with the seat before slowly descending, perched delicately on the edge. Once seated, the corset enforced an upright posture, with the shoulder braces preventing any slouching. Her legs, concealed by the voluminous skirts, were gently pressed together by the underskirt, the fabrics rustling softly as she adjusted to find a modicum of comfort. Julien then leaned in to adjust the skirts, ensuring they draped elegantly around her, providing a final touch to her poised presentation.
After that, she was pretty much stuck, arranged in her seat, upright and presenting herself to Julien seated opposite. She would be looking at him, or rather at his hands. The Gowbao Yoohoo locked her head into a position looking forward and downward, and she was unable to turn it without turning her full body. She was also unable to lift her head much, and would be looking at him by turning her eyes upwards for a moment and looking through the lashes of her eyes. Her pose lent itself naturally to placing her gloved hands folded into her lap, keeping the knees under her skirt closely together, both feet planted firmly next to each other under her perched position.
This moment, with Julien tending to her every need, underscored Anna’s feeling of being intensely cared for. However, it was more than that; it was a manifestation of her choice, her control. By choosing this outfit, Anna had embraced a form of self-expression that was as restrictive as it was liberating. Like a poet choosing the constraints of a sonnet to convey depth and emotion, Anna used the limitations of her dress to craft her image and control how she was perceived. The restrictions made her more dependent on Julien, but she appreciated how this closeness enhanced their connection.
Julien ordered food without consulting her, knowing her preferences and making it a point to remember them. What might have once bothered her about losing this bit of autonomy now felt right.
After a dinner filled with soft glances and tender care, the world around them seemed to quieten to a whisper. Feeling the warmth of the evening envelop her, Anna noticed Julien’s demeanor shift to something more serious. As he gently took her gloved hand in his, anticipation built within her, a tender fluttering that seemed to echo in the air between them.
“Miss Anna,” Julien said, his voice filled with emotion that instantly captured her attention, “being with you has brought such happiness and peace into my life. Your grace, dedication, and spirit have completely won me over. I can’t imagine my future without you by my side.”
He paused, looking deeply into her eyes, the unspoken question hanging in the air. Then, with a gentleness that matched the seriousness of his words, he asked, “Would you do me the honor of becoming my ward? Let’s share this journey, build a life together filled with respect and love. If you say yes, I’ll ask your father for his blessing, to cherish and care for you all our days.”
Overwhelmed by the sincerity and depth of Julien’s proposal, Anna felt a profound joy spreading through her. Her heart full, she found her voice and simply said, “Yes, Sir.”
By saying yes, Anna accepted the world the way it had become. She knew being Julien’s ward meant embracing her role and following the new rules. But she felt at peace with this. The idea of being Julien’s “Good Girl” and living up to expectations felt right. She saw it as bringing honor to her family and continuing their legacy. Julien had always taken good care of her, and with him, she felt safe.
The thought of facing this changed world without Julien was daunting. His care and understanding made her feel secure. By accepting his proposal, Anna was choosing the path laid out by society. She believed that with Julien, she could find happiness even in a world shaped by the virus.

title: Chapter 13: A Giving-Away Ceremony
content:
A Giving-Away Ceremony# As Anna planned her giving-away ceremony, her emotions were all over the place. The private talk between Julien and her father had gone smoothly, following the customs of their Changed society. When she heard her father agreed, she felt a deep sense of gratitude and responsibility. This was more than just a formality—it was a promise to uphold the values and traditions that shaped their lives.
Anna chose “The Jade Garden” for the ceremony, a venue that captured the peace and beauty she wanted for her union with Julien. Nestled in the serene landscape north of Geneva, the tea house was famous for its beautiful gardens and calming atmosphere. It was the perfect setting for the start of their life together, where the natural elegance mirrored their deep commitment.
For her outfit, Anna picked a blend of traditional Changed dress with modern touches of Chinese Hanfu. This choice showed her personal style and her respect for tradition, as well as her openness to the evolving nature of their society. Her corset and Yoyah Sheengzoh beneath the elegant layers symbolized her commitment to the ideals of Changed womanhood, showing her readiness to embrace her new responsibilities and joys.
During the official ceremony, her father would hand her over to Julien, marking her transition from “Marc Lefèvre’s Anna” to “Julien Moreau’s Anna,” to whom she would then owe her loyalty. The tea ceremony Anna planned for Julien afterward was more than a ritual; it was a promise of her dedication to their future together. The celebration would be held in the beautiful surroundings of The Jade Garden. The guest list was small, including those who had been pillars of support and love in their lives. Anna hoped her dear friend Sonia could attend, her presence a symbol of the enduring friendship that had supported them through the changes in their world.
The wedding, set for eight weeks away, was a beacon of hope for Anna. She saw it as a way to unite tradition and love in a changing world.

title: Chapter 14: In Shanghai
content:
Storycodes Mf, FF, bdsm, con, mind-control, submission, humiliation, conditioning, corsetry, hobble-skirts, retro-femininity, silence, masks, obedience, correction, arranged-marriage, ritual, giving-away, tea-ceremony, dystopia
Disguised as a maid in Shanghai, Sonia submits to corsets, collars, and silence to spy on the man who built the virus. Returning to Geneva, Sonia balances rebellion and temptation as Anna embraces marriage, ritual, and the virus’s vision of harmony. Sonia’s mission takes her deep into Shanghai, where the Change has already transformed public life into a theater of corsets, masks, and ritualized silence. To get close to Dr. Cheng, she buries her pride beneath maid’s uniforms and enforced etiquette, every gesture rehearsed, every word stolen from her by a porcelain mask. The deeper she plays the role, the more the role plays her, testing her resolve and eroding her sense of self. Returning to Geneva with stolen secrets, Sonia finds her city equally transformed, her closest friend Anna serenely preparing for her giving-away ceremony. With data that could expose the truth but a society that welcomes its own restraint, Sonia must decide whether she is resisting for others—or resisting alone.
Back from Shanghai with stolen data, Sonia learns the virus is more than a tool of control—it rewrites memory itself, weaving new traditions and loyalties into the very fabric of society. While she struggles with masks, corsets, and the lure of support in a world that anticipates her every need, her friend Anna prepares joyfully for her Giving-Away, serenely pledging obedience to Julien and to the Changed ideals. Sonia, caught between resistance and belonging, must decide whether to cling to her autonomy or accept the peace that Anna offers her in the form of a vial that would complete her transformation.
In Shanghai# Sonia stepped off the plane into Shanghai’s humid air, immediately feeling the weight of change around her. The airport hummed with efficiency, but there was an undercurrent of formality that prickled her skin. Women moved with precise steps, their bodies cinched at the waist by corsets, and men carried themselves with newfound rigidity.
She breezed through luggage claim and customs, her eyes taking in every detail. Shanghai was even further along than Geneva; the Change here felt more… complete. Sonia steeled herself, realizing she’d have to tread carefully if she wanted to fit in without losing sight of her mission.
A Mirende Gingciao boutique caught her eye as she exited towards the taxi stand. She hesitated, then pushed open the door. The bell chimed softly behind her as she stepped inside, the scent of fresh fabric and polished wood filling her nostrils.
The saleswoman greeted her with a polite bow, her own corset creaking slightly as she moved. “Welcome to Mirende Gingciao,” she said, her voice pitched higher than usual. “How may we assist you today?”
Sonia approached the rack, running her fingers along the silks and laces. She picked up a deep blue corset and held it against herself in the mirror. It was beautiful, but it felt like admitting defeat.
“I need something… suitable,” she said, choosing her words carefully. “For business meetings.”
The saleswoman nodded knowingly. “Of course,” she replied, selecting a Gowbao Yoohoo blouse to pair with the corset. “This one is designed for self-donning, perfect for evenings out or formal events.”
Sonia took the garments, her resolve wavering. But this was just surface deep, she told herself. She wasn’t changing who she was inside; she was simply playing a part.
With that thought, she made her way to the fitting room, leaving her old self behind the door. For now, she’d be another woman in Shanghai - corseted, restrained, and Changed on the outside. But her heart still burned with determination to undo the Change.
She had to undress down to her lowest layer, a cotton spaghetti-strap top, over which the corset would go. The stiff front busk closed with seven steel hooks, and she grabbed the laces behind her, feeling for the crossed laces at the top and bottom. Pulling each “X” gradually tightened the corset, working her way downwards and upwards to the to the waist where the loose laces could then be pulled to pick up the slack. The first iteration made the corset feel snug, and she could feel the posture it imposed on her. She arranged her breasts into the cups, which provided some serious uplift and positioning, and following tightening passes turned snugness into serious pressure, holding her upright.
After fastening the garters, the Yoyah Sheengzoh went back on over it. It hugged her legs tightly, the reinforced hem a barrier against wider steps. Experimentally, she took a few cautious strides, feeling the fabric catch and hold her knees together.
She then proceeded to put on her new Gowbao Yoohoo. The blouse was a simple silk design with an internally boned mandarin collar extending up to the back of her head and buttons that reached from her right shoulder to the collar. Closing the buttons from the shoulder upward, the collar gradually tightened around her neck like a corset, It was regal, yes, but restrictive too. Any attempt to look up or turn her head met with resistance and eventually became painful.
The ensemble was completed with a Chinese-style narrow overskirt, much like a pencil skirt, covering the Yoyah Sheengzoh. Confused by the new sensations of restriction imposed by her dress, she almost forgot her hat, purse, and gloves, turning around and shuffling back to the changing room to retrieve them. She had to bend at the knees because the corset and blouse effectively prevented her from bending any other way.
In her new attire, Sonia immediately felt a shift in her posture and movement, serving as a constant, unspoken reminder of the Change’s influence. The relentless pressure of the corset and the neck corset of the blouse imposed the same posture on her as that shared by all the Changed around her. Each step and breath reminded her of the concessions she had made, fueling a mix of resignation and resistance within her. While the attire was a tool for blending in, it also symbolized the very phenomenon she aimed to resist and possibly undo. Her movements, now dictated by the confines of her new wardrobe, mirrored the controlled elegance of those around her, reflecting the deep and personal impact of the Change on individuals and society.
During her journey to the Campanile Shanghai Jing’an Hotel via the subway, Sonia observed the diversity among the Changed around her. Despite the fact that their attire was uniformly restrictive—corsets, high-collared Gobao Yoohoo blouses, hobbling underskirts, and high-heeled shoes were mandatory—the outfits were a blend of Victorian styles, New Look ideas, and uniquely local Chinese-influenced designs. Gloves were a universal accessory, varying from delicate lace to more practical leather, apparently depending on the wearer’s needs or tasks. Heels clicked harshly on the subway floor, each pair thoughtfully chosen to complement the wearer’s ensemble. Hair coverings varied—some women wore stylish hijabs matching their outfits, while others opted for local Chinese head coverings or fashionable hats, each adding a personal touch to the uniformity prescribed by their Changed status.
Men favored sharp business suits or slightly more casual attire. Their suits were impeccably tailored, with narrow waists and broad shoulders, projecting an air of authority and control. Casual wear, while less formal, still adhered to a neat, polished aesthetic, with tucked-in shirts and cuffed trousers paired with pristine loafers or brogues.
After a lengthy journey of nearly an hour and a half, Sonia arrived at Jing’an Temple station, retrieved her luggage, and made her way to the Campanile Shanghai Jing’an Hotel. Once checked in, she eagerly shed her restrictive attire. Peeling off the high-collared blouse and stepping out of her confining Yoyah Sheengzoh, she breathed a sigh of relief. Sonia carefully untied the bow of her corset laces, gradually easing the tightness around her waist. She then slipped off her stockings and garters, quickly headed into the bathroom for a refreshing shower, and collapsed into bed, utterly spent from the flight.
The next morning, following breakfast, she began to delve into Dr. Mingyu Cheng’s background. As she pieced together information, the details of Dr. Cheng’s life painted a picture of a man with both the means and expertise to have engineered LASS-VASH to cause the Change. From his humble beginnings as an American-born Chinese to his ascendancy among Shanghai’s biotech elite, every detail seemed to underscore his capability for such a monumental undertaking.
Dr. Cheng was well known for his work in neurophysiology and biotechnology. He had an illustrious career that took him from the academic circles of New York to the forefront of Shanghai’s elite. He was the founder of Cheng Biotech Industries (CBI), and his work had revolutionized the treatment of neurological disorders, propelling him to billionaire status. He reportedly lived in the upscale Xuhui District.
As Sonia delved deeper into Dr. Cheng’s life, she felt awe, but also revulsion. The idea that one individual could wield such enormous influence, reshaping the very essence of society and personal identity, was both intriguing and terrifying. Despite her disdain for the Change, Sonia couldn’t help but admire the sheer brilliance and audacity required to conceive and execute such a sweeping plan.
Realizing the elusive nature of Shanghai’s elite, Sonia understood that direct approaches would be fruitless. The city protected its secrets diligently, especially those involving prominent figures like Dr. Cheng. It dawned on her that her best chance to infiltrate Cheng’s world was to become part of the unseen workforce that maintained the luxurious lifestyles of the wealthy.
She needed to become a maid.

title: Chapter 15: Maid in Training
Chapter 16: A Maid's work
content:
A Maid’s work# Sonia applied for the position, presenting herself as the perfect candidate. The interview process went quickly, either due to her qualifications or the efficiency of the Cheng household. Once she got the job, she felt triumph, but also apprehension. It was a unique chance to advance her mission, but it meant diving deeper into a lifestyle she had resisted.
Moving into the small, plain maid’s room in the attic of Dr. Cheng’s villa, Sonia faced the reality of her new life. The room, bare and impersonal, starkly reminded her of her role. Her few functional belongings underscored her commitment to her mission. As she arranged her things, she felt a deep sense of isolation. She was part of the household now, yet remained an outsider, a spy in a world both foreign and crucial to her quest.
Living in Dr. Cheng’s mansion, Sonia found herself in a stricter, more anonymous setting than her training. Each morning, as she put on her uniform, the reflection in the mirror sparked a sense of loss. The corset, with its shoulder braces, forced her body into a rigid form, while the narrow underskirt severely limited her movements. The ankle-length gray maid’s dress, with a high collar and gloves, erased any trace of personal identity, allowing her to blend into the background.
Roll call became a daily ritual of conformity. Lined up with the other maids, Sonia stood for inspection, her makeup flawlessly applied to meet the household’s high standards. This routine highlighted the erosion of her individuality, a necessary sacrifice for her ultimate goal.
Inside Dr. Cheng’s mansion, Sonia moved like a shadow, unnoticed among the other uniformed staff. She had no name or identity; she was just a maid, a role performing services. Silent, but useful and pleasant to the eye.
Discipline was strict. In public spaces, Sonia had to be silent, impeccably dressed, and either working or waiting for orders, standing discreetly by a door or table. As Mei Lin had trained her, she couldn’t allow herself to relax. Her mind stayed focused on her superiors, ready to serve at any moment. The strictness of her uniform helped, constantly reminding her whenever she relaxed her shoulders or slouched—behaviors that would lead to discipline if noticed.
Sonia struggled not to lose herself in the monotonous routines of service. It was easy for her mind to drift, focusing only on immediate tasks and the sensory input from her uniform, adapting to its constraints. She concentrated on the person she served; their identity mattered no more than her own. She existed only to serve.
The housekeeper, Mrs. Huang, managed the staff with an iron fist. Her sharp commands sliced through the air. She was a stern woman, always watching closely, quick to point out any imperfection. “You missed a spot, Su ni ya. Do it again, and this time, pretend your job depends on it, because it does!” her voice would echo down the hallways, making the newer maids jump.
The butler, Mr. Chen, while equally strict, maintained an air of polite formality. “Miss Sonia, if you would kindly ensure that the silver is polished to a mirror finish. We aim for excellence in all things here,” he would say, his tone firm yet wrapped in a veneer of civility, underscoring his demand for perfection.
Within the vast quiet of Dr. Cheng’s mansion, Sonia was nearly invisible, her voice reduced to a mantra of submission. “Yes, sir,” “Of course, sir,” and “Is there anything else this humble maid can do for you, sir?” These phrases echoed only when directly addressed by her employer or his guests. She remained silent unless spoken to. When referring to herself, she used her role, never the first person—she was not “I” nor “Sonia”; she was “this humble maid.”
Among the staff, communication often unfolded through a silent ballet of gestures and movements, a language Sonia found surprisingly familiar. They used 手舞言, Show-woo-yen, or “Showyou,” the hand-dancing language. It was a tool she wielded with unexpected grace, another unforeseen gift from the virus that had altered her in so many ways.
Work took her to all parts of the large building, and Sonia quickly memorized the sprawling layout of Dr. Cheng’s mansion, committing the twists and turns of its opulent corridors to memory. She noted the locations of key areas, like Dr. Cheng’s personal office and the laboratory spaces. Both were off-limits to staff unless for specific tasks like special cleaning or supply runs, and only under direct orders.
One crisp morning, Sonia received a summons from Mrs. Huang. “You are to retrieve a briefcase from Dr. Cheng’s quarters and deliver it to the conference room. Do not dally,” Mrs. Huang instructed, her tone leaving no room for argument.
With the rapid clicking of her heels through the narrow servant corridors, Sonia navigated to Dr. Cheng’s private quarters, entering through a hidden servant’s door. She found the briefcase on a small desk in his bedroom, heavy with papers and a tablet. Grabbing it, she hurried back to the conference room, her steps tiny and quick, panting against the tightness of her corset. She paused behind the servant’s entrance to catch her breath, smoothing her skirts to fix her appearance, then entered the conference room. Dr. Cheng was deep in discussion with his team of genetic engineers. Placing the briefcase beside him, Sonia retreated to the wall, blending into the ornate decor while keeping her senses alert.
Dr. Cheng’s voice filled the room, his passion for his vision evident. “We are on the brink of a new era,” he declared, discussing how the Change was meant to foster a collectivist society to address global issues like climate change and inequality. His words, filled with idealism, struck Sonia as ironic coming from a man of such wealth.
As the conversation turned to technical aspects and timelines, Sonia remained perfectly still, her training keeping her attentive yet unobtrusive. The stiffness of her attire, with the corset compressing her torso and the blouse collar grazing her chin, made even small movements feel laborious. Yet, she performed her role flawlessly, moving only to serve drinks or adjust settings at the slightest indication—a nod, a gesture.
Dr. Cheng outlined the timeline for the Changed to influence laws upholding societal norms. “When do we anticipate reaching the infiltration threshold needed to begin legal transformations?” he asked pointedly. The engineers scrambled through their data, providing estimates and scenarios that painted a future reshaped by their work.
Throughout the meeting, Sonia’s emotions swung between awe at the scope of Dr. Cheng’s ambitions and a growing resolve to stop them. The realization that she was privy to a plan seeking to alter human society fundamentally was chilling. Every discussion about timelines and societal changes, every casual reference to the deep and permanent impact of the Change, reinforced her determination to expose the truth.
As the meeting adjourned and Dr. Cheng and his team left the room, Sonia lingered under the pretense of cleaning up, her mind racing with the information she had gathered. Exiting the conference room, Sonia’s steps were careful, the whisper of her skirts and the click of her heels echoing softly in the empty hallway. She was more than just a maid in a billionaire’s mansion; she was a spy at the heart of an operation that could decide the fate of humanity. Reminding herself of her mission, Sonia kept her eyes and ears open for any snippet of conversation or overlooked document. Anything that might lead her closer to understanding the true nature of the virus that had changed the world and forced her to become… this.
One afternoon, Mr. Chen called Sonia over. “Miss Sonia, Dr. Cheng wants his office floors waxed tonight. You’ll handle it yourself,” he said, handing her the keys with a nod to show the task’s importance. Dr. Cheng was not present that day; he had gone to a new fashion show by Mirende Ginciao, one of the few things that could draw him away from his sanctuary. It seemed to be a big event, introducing a major new fashion item.
Seeing her chance, Sonia used her role as a maid to slip into the lab under the guise of her duties. Inside, she moved quickly, her gloved hands searching through the lab despite the restrictions of her outfit. She opened drawers and flipped through files, balancing speed with the need to stay unnoticed. Her pulse quickened when she found USB sticks hidden among the lab’s clutter.
She transferred the files to her phone with speed and precision. Each copied file brought her closer to understanding, another piece of the puzzle that had led her halfway around the world. The fabric of her dress brushed against her skin as she moved, a constant reminder of the world she was fighting against.
Sonia’s heart raced as she heard Dr. Cheng return, her actions in the lab just moments away from discovery. With practiced submissiveness, she curtsied, the stiffness of her uniform sharply reminding her of her role in this elaborate act. Her exit from the lab was as quiet as a whisper, leaving Dr. Cheng unaware of the theft that had just occurred right under his nose. Once back in her small, spartan room, Sonia felt the weight of her corset and the high collar of her uniform. Her phone, filled with stolen secrets, lay in her hands. The files she had transferred spoke of a virus meant not just to infect bodies but to reshape society with forced ideals. Sonia’s mind raced as she uploaded everything to the cloud, carefully making another copy of the encrypted data on her phone.
Approaching Mrs. Huang cautiously, Sonia spoke, her voice trembling slightly. “Mrs. Huang, Madam, if I may,” Sonia began, eyes lowered. “My mother is gravely ill, and I humbly ask for some time off to care for her.”
Mrs. Huang, ever the strict overseer, arched an eyebrow, her expression stern. “Su ni ya,” she said sharply, “you know the rules. Your duties here come first. Personal issues can’t interfere.”
Just as Mrs. Huang was about to refuse, Mr. Chen, the butler, entered the room. He had overheard the conversation, and his demeanor was one of controlled concern, reflecting the Changed values on family importance. “Mrs. Huang, may I have a word?” he asked smoothly, his voice calm yet authoritative.
“Of course, Mr. Chen,” Mrs. Huang replied, her tone shifting to one of deference to her immediate superior in the household hierarchy.
Mr. Chen turned to Sonia, serious. “Miss Sonia,” he began, “while your primary duty is here, we must remember the core values Dr. Cheng instills in us, including family. You may take time to attend to your mother. However, remember, you are an extension of this household’s values, even outside these walls.”
“Thank you, sir,” Sonia responded, curtsying. “I appreciate your understanding and promise to uphold our standards and represent this household with respect and dedication.” The lies slipped smoothly from her lips.
Mr. Chen nodded, a subtle smile softening his stern features. “See that you do, Sonia. We consider you part of this family too. I expect you to carry yourself as a member of this household should, even in personal trials. Go, attend to your mother, and return with dignity.”
Sonia curtsied deeply, her heart racing from the lie. “Thank you sincerely, sir. I won’t disappoint you or this esteemed household.”
As Sonia left the room, her mind raced through her escape plan, knowing every second Mrs. Huang and Mr. Chen remained unaware of her permanent departure was precious time to reach safety.
Sonia booked a flight home with urgency. She had no intention to formally quit or return, relying on the protection of her faked credentials and the distance she intended to put between herself and Dr. Cheng’s household. The data on her phone, now encrypted and stored in the cloud, was a key that could unlock the truth about the virus and its creators.
Landside at the airport, Sonia’s eyes caught a display that chilled her to the core. It was a showcase from Mirende Ginciao, the high-fashion boutique known for its restrictive designs. These accessories were the reason Dr. Cheng had been away. The display featured a new line of masks called Jinshuwan—simple yet sinister half-masks covering the mouth and nose, stretching from ear to ear. They were marketed as affordable and practical, made from lightweight materials, less intimidating but no less controlling.
Next to them were the luxurious Jurenmuse masks. These were full-face masks, beautifully crafted from porcelain and fine materials, polished to a reflective shine. They left only the eyes visible, turning wearers into living statues, objects of silent beauty. Each mask came with a bit-gag, a built-in silicone silencer inserted into the mouth. Unlike traditional masks, these stayed in place by the gag, ensuring silence was both compulsory and conspicuous.
The significance of these masks hit Sonia hard—the silence, the forced submission, the erasure of identity. It was a chilling confirmation of the society’s push for total control, especially over women. The use of Showyou, the hand-dancing language she shared with the maids, suddenly made frightening sense. What seemed a discreet way to communicate was part of a larger plan to silence women’s voices altogether.
Standing there, staring at the display, Sonia felt anger mixed with fear. She muttered to herself, a blend of horror and resolve. “This… this is their plan. Complete silence, total submission. They’ve moved from shaping bodies to sealing lips, erasing personal expression. And we… we’ve been part of this without knowing.”
The bit gags were a brutal twist. “They’re not just taking away our ability to speak; they’re physically gagging us, making us complicit in our own silencing. These gags… they’re a physical manifestation of the virus’s metaphorical muzzle.”

It doesn’t just infect; it rewrites and imprints new memories and values directly into the brain’s neural pathways,” Anna explained, her admiration for the design evident.
“This way,” she continued, “it doesn’t force its new behaviors on the person. Instead, they are remembered, and the human brain wraps them in existing memories of how these behaviors were learned, modifying existing memories to fit. Changed have age-old traditions, rules and rituals, because they remember these things as something they have always had. At the same time, the old memories are forgotten, and the fact that the old behaviors and rules are seen as shameful helps a lot.”
Sonia listened intently as Anna continued. “The genome is predominantly data, an imprint. Additionally, it contains compulsory behaviors. They are tailored specifically to affect the infected based on their sex. The compulsion to serve and submit is activated only in females. Males are affected by a different set of values and compulsions,” Anna explained, simultaneously signing a mix of professionalism and awe.
Anna showed Sonia the data on her laptop, pointing out the important parts. She moved easily, still a skilled scientist, but her signing showed she had accepted her new life. “It’s… elegant, the way it brings harmony, order. I couldn’t have designed it better myself,” Anna admitted, her gaze meeting Sonia’s. They were very different now—Anna admired the virus, and Sonia wanted to fight it.
Sonia experienced a whirlwind of emotions. The virus was complex and deeply integrated into society, but Anna’s insights offered a glimmer of hope. They could use Anna’s discoveries to combat the virus. Realizing that Anna could still utilize her scientific expertise was crucial, and Sonia saw it as a vital tool in their fight. Faced with numerous challenges, Sonia felt emboldened by the new knowledge and Anna’s support. Together, she resolved to find a way to undermine the virus’s influence with Anna’s help, targeting one genetic sequence at a time.

title: Chapter 21: Living in a Changed Society
content:
Living in a Changed Society# Several weeks into her endeavor of trying to blend in better, Sonia found that her adjustments had begun to feel… almost normal.
Though initially foreign and uncomfortable, she had become accustomed to the ritual of lacing on her underbust corset before bed. What was once a task she approached with reluctance now brought an unexpected sense of security. The absence of its constrictive embrace made her feel exposed and vulnerable. The transition from her day corset, a formidable S-bend that sculpted her figure into the accepted silhouette, to the slightly more forgiving night corset had become a daily ritual.
It felt normal too that her hands now danced with a fluid grace that came naturally. Gone was the clumsy and jerky signaling she had used when she first picked up hand-dancing again after returning from Shanghai. The act of curtsying, a gesture she often had performed ironically when she was a maid, had woven itself into her interactions so seamlessly that its absence now felt like an oversight, a breach of an unspoken contract between her and the world she navigated. As she stood before the mirror, masked and corseted, Sonia saw her reflection staring back at her. The woman in the mirror moved with practiced elegance, her gestures refined, her posture demure.
She recalled a recent encounter at a bookstore where a man had reached for a volume on the top shelf for her. His actions were gentle, protective, and anticipated her needs before she could even express them. Sonia had curtsied instinctively, a silent “thank you,” and had felt a rush of gratitude for the simple act of kindness. This exchange had felt surprisingly natural, even right.
Similar situations happened every day, multiple times a day: in the tram, at work, out when shopping or in the café, everywhere someone, usually a man, was around her and helped her before she could even realize that she needed assistance. Her clothing, restrictive as it was, should be hindering her, but in every situation where this would be the case, some man was present in time, courteously helping her to effortlessly and elegantly navigate the situation. Doors opened before her when she was in a restrictive or voluminous skirt, chairs moved behind her when she was about to sit down, and things she could not reach materialized in her hands whenever she thought of reaching for them. Seats in the tram were offered to her, and hands of strangers helped her board the tram or disembark.
Men at work organized meetings and functions in a way that took women in corsets and demanding high heels into account, and thus she was able to walk wooden planks across a soft lawn in her heels on the GAIA summer party, and found convenient clusters of high-backed chairs at her disposal to rest her feet. When she intended to sit down on them, a random colleague was present to push the chair as she sat down, making her restrained movements elegant. She was bound, helpless and mute in her clothing, and it was… convenient?
The situation at work developed similarly, and in ways that Sonia had not anticipated. In her office at GAIA, Sonia sat on her Balans kneeling stool, which she found better suited to her narrow underskirt than any chair. Her corseted form reflected in the sleek surface of her workstation, she contemplated the paradoxes that had become her daily reality. The mask that concealed her facial expressions and the gloves that sheathed her hands—each element, initially a symbol of constraint, had seamlessly integrated into her professional life in ways she never anticipated.
Typing with gloved fingers was a challenge Sonia initially met with frustration. Each keystroke felt like a battle, the tactile disconnect rendering her once-fluent movements clumsy and uncertain. However, over time, she adapted, finding rhythms and methods that mitigated the barrier imposed by the gloves. The nuisance of removing them became so irritating that it had turned into a ritual she seldom performed. The sensation of being unprotected now evoked visceral discomfort, a strong dislike of her bare skin exposed to the unseen filth of the world.
In meetings, the dynamics had shifted dramatically. The once chaotic exchanges, mostly with men speaking over each other, had transformed into a structured ballet of gestures and allocated turns. Sonia recalled the times before the Change when she struggled to be heard—a sharp contrast to the present, where each woman, masked and silent, waited for her designated moment to contribute via hand-dancing. The men, in turn, had adapted to this regime, focusing their attention on interpreting the gestures, ensuring that the women’s inputs were not just seen but understood.
The enforced order, a product of the Changed’s adherence to submission and structured interaction, had paradoxically created a space where women’s contributions were guaranteed equal weight and consideration. Sonia realized that these practices, which she had viewed as regressive and antithetical to feminism, had inadvertently leveled the academic playing field. She recalled a recent project meeting where her hand-dancing suggestions were met with nods of approval and thoughtful consideration. The absence of verbal interruptions and the focused attention on her gestured input underscored a sense of professional respect she had not fully appreciated before.
Sonia found herself at a crossroads of thought, recognizing the efficacy and fairness these Changed practices had introduced into her work environment. The irony was not lost on her: the restrictions she resisted had fostered an unexpected form of empowerment within the academic arena. But this acknowledgment was tinged with lingering dissonance. The gains in effectiveness and equality were overshadowed by the loss of vocal expression, a trade-off that Sonia continued to grapple with every time she felt the tug of the mask and the silicone ball in her mouth.
Sonia was forced to reassess her understanding of feminism, effectiveness, and autonomy. The realization that freedom could take many forms, and that empowerment could emerge from unexpected sources, was a journey of discovery that challenged her preconceptions.
Navigating through her day, Sonia was acutely aware of the constraints her clothing imposed, and also of the weird new social status indicators the Changed had. The buttons on her dresses were at the shoulder, not at the back as with other women: she had to be able to dress alone, without assistance from a man or a maid. Her billowing and restrictive skirts made certain tasks daunting, if not impossible, without assistance. But men were often there, anticipating her needs before she could even articulate them.
This dependence, Sonia reflected, was not the kind of helplessness she feared but a form of interdependence that the Changed society fostered. Men, conditioned to be ever attentive and supportive, engaged with her in a non-verbal dance of gestures and anticipation. It was parallel to the hand-dancing that had become her voice, each act a thread in the fabric of a collectivist society that prized harmony and mutual support over individual autonomy.
Sonia struggled to find a term for the unique form of intimacy these everyday interactions bred. It was an intimacy born of necessity, a constant connection that was surprisingly comforting. The realization that she was never truly alone “out there,” that the societal structure ensured she was supported, brought both comfort and a lingering question about the nature of autonomy. The only time she was ever alone was at home, in her apartment, where the silence and stillness offered a stark contrast to the orchestrated interactions of her public life. Sonia contemplated the idea that perhaps being alone, being autonomous in the way she once cherished, was anathema to the Changed ethos. The solitude she once sought now felt like an aberration, a deviation from the collective embrace of society. Was autonomy then not about independence but about finding one’s place within the web of societal support and mutual dependency? Sonia resolved to ask Anna more and more detailed questions about “living as Changed.”
