With careful precision, Rose removed the sack-like nightgown, its narrow cut restricting Charlotte’s legs. Next came the night corset, extending from Charlotte’s knees to her bust line. The release from its confines brought a fleeting moment of freedom, allowing Charlotte to stretch her limbs and breathe more deeply. Rose undid the mittens and the heel-less night boots that forced Charlotte’s feet into an en-pointe position.
Charlotte sat up, rubbing her wrists where the mittens had chafed. “Thank you,” she murmured, a trace of surprise in her voice at the unexpected kindness.
“Let’s get you washed up,” Rose suggested, guiding Charlotte to the washbasin. The cool water was a welcome relief, and Charlotte splashed her face, savoring the brief taste of autonomy.
“Feels good to be able to move,” Charlotte admitted, her eyes meeting Rose’s in the mirror.
“We don’t have much time, so let’s make it count,” Rose replied, offering a conspiratorial smile as she began the lengthy process of preparing Charlotte for the day.
As Rose worked, she spoke softly, her words carrying a weight that made Charlotte pause. “I need to tell you something, Miss Hargreaves. I’m no maid. Like you, I was once a girl at the reformatory.”
Charlotte’s eyes widened with intrigue. “You were?”
Rose nodded, her expression serious. “You should be able to tell from my waist alone. Mrs. Blackthorn’s cruelty is something I know all too well. I’m here because I need your help. I want revenge, and I thought you might, too.”
Charlotte’s interest was piqued, and she nodded, her resolve hardening. “I do. I hate her.”
“Good,” Rose said, a glint of determination in her eyes. “Tonight, at the ball, I can spice Mrs. Blackthorn’s tea with laudanum. Once she’s under, you’ll have your chance to be alone with her. Do with her as you wish. But I need to know you’re committed to this.”
Charlotte’s eyes lit with a mix of hope and malice. “Really? And you’ll give me more laudanum?”
“Enough to take the edge off for you, too,” Rose promised, lacing the corset tighter still. “But you must be careful—our chance depends on subtlety.”
Charlotte exhaled sharply as the stays pulled her waist into an impossibly tight silhouette. Her gown for the ball, a lavish creation of deep blue satin, awaited beside the bed. Its high neckline and delicate lace trim painted a picture of elegance, but the truth was evident in the restrictive cut and impeccably boned structure.
“I want to see her brought down,” Charlotte confessed, her voice low.
“Then we have an agreement,” Rose said, a hint of triumph in her tone as she tied off the final lace. “Now, let’s make sure you’re the belle of the ball. They’ll never see you coming.”
As Charlotte stood, her posture rigid from the corset’s grip, she felt the spark of defiance reignite within her.
As Rose, Seraphina navigated her duties throughout the day with careful precision, narrowly escaping exposure. In the grand drawing room, Mrs. Blackthorn sat poised with a cup of tea, her sharp eyes observing the staff as they moved about. Rose approached with a tray of biscuits, her heart thudding beneath her tightly laced uniform.
“Your waist is quite admirable, dear,” Mrs. Blackthorn remarked, her gaze lingering on Rose’s silhouette. “What is your name?”
“Rose, ma’am,” Seraphina replied, keeping her voice steady.
Mrs. Blackthorn peered closely at her face, a glimmer of suspicion in her expression. Rose held her breath, hoping the layers of makeup would hold. After a moment, Mrs. Blackthorn nodded, seemingly satisfied, and returned her attention to her tea.
The evening arrived, and the ballroom at the Langham Hotel was a vision of opulence. Crystal chandeliers cast a warm glow over the polished floors, and a string quartet played softly in the background. The invited guests, a mix of young, wealthy, single men with particular interests and a few accompanying matrons or parents, mingled with anticipation.
Rose moved deftly through the crowd, balancing a tray of pastries and light drinks with practiced ease. Her eyes flitted over the guests, noting their expressions and lingering glances as they observed the preparations.
The processional entrance of the girls was announced, and a hush fell over the room. Mrs. Blackthorn stood at the top of the grand staircase, overseeing the proceedings with an air of authority. One by one, the girls descended the stairs, their gowns resplendent in the candlelight.
At the bottom of the stair, she curtsied gracefully and took her place along the edge of the ballroom. The men watched from across the room, their eyes attentive and appraising.
Mrs. Blackthorn stepped forward, her voice carrying over the hushed assembly. “Esteemed patrons of Loch Thorne, it is my pleasure to welcome you to our annual ball. Tonight, we celebrate the accomplishments of these young ladies in discipline, composure, and feminine restraint.”
A murmur of approval rippled through the crowd, and Mrs. Blackthorn extended her hand to a distinguished gentleman standing nearby. “May I present Lord Everingham, a loyal patron of our reformatory.”
Lord Everingham, a titled gentleman of considerable influence, bowed with a dignified air. “The pleasure is mine, Mrs. Blackthorn.”
The quartet struck up a lively tune, and Mrs. Blackthorn led Lord Everingham onto the floor for the first waltz. Despite her lacing and the restrictive gown, Mrs. Blackthorn moved in step with Lord Everingham, which set the tone and pace for the evening.
Midway through the dance, the invited gentlemen began to join in, each approaching a girl to ask for the honor of a dance. The ballroom filled with the sound of laughter and conversation as the couples twirled gracefully across the floor. The lively pace of the dance took its toll on Mrs. Blackthorn, who graciously thanked Lord Everingham for the dance, pausing afterward to catch her breath. Her cheeks were flushed, and she fanned herself lightly.
“An invigorating waltz, Lord Everingham,” she remarked with a polite smile, “though it seems I am not quite as youthful as my charges.”
“Indeed, Mrs. Blackthorn, but you are as graceful as ever,” Lord Everingham replied, offering a courteous bow before retreating to the sidelines.
Rose approached with impeccable timing, carrying a delicate china cup filled with tea. The steam carried the rich aroma of spices, masking the laudanum she had generously laced into the brew.
“Some tea, ma’am?” Rose offered with a perfect curtsy.
“Bless you, girl,” Mrs. Blackthorn murmured, accepting the cup with gratitude. She sipped it eagerly, the heat and flavor providing a welcome respite. “Delightful, truly. Just what I needed.”
Rose nodded, her expression demure. “I’m glad it pleases you, ma’am.”
As the minutes passed, Rose kept a watchful eye on Mrs. Blackthorn, noting the subtle changes in her demeanor. The older woman’s movements grew languid, her eyelids drooping ever so slightly. When she swayed on her feet, Rose was at her side in an instant, a steadying presence.
“Feeling a bit dizzy, ma’am?” Rose inquired, feigning concern.
Mrs. Blackthorn blinked, her composure slipping. “Yes, perhaps… perhaps a moment to rest is in order.”
“Allow me to assist you, ma’am,” Rose insisted gently, guiding her towards the exit. “You’ve been skipping meals again, I wager.” As she left the room, Rose discreetly gestured to Charlotte, who had been lingering near the entrance, waiting for her cue.
On the way to the salon to retire for a moment, Mrs. Blackthorn chuckled, her inhibitions loosening with each step. “Oh, Rose, your waist is quite exceptional,” she remarked, her words slurring slightly. “The very ideal my institution strives to produce. So natural, so… impeccable.”
Rose smiled modestly as she led Mrs. Blackthorn up a discreet staircase to a small salon on the next floor. The space was quiet, removed from the noise of the ballroom below.
“Let’s have you rest here, ma’am,” Rose suggested, easing Mrs. Blackthorn into a plush chair. “Miss Hargreaves here will assist you.”
“Miss Hargreaves,” Rose beckoned with a fake smile. “Mrs. Blackthorn needs a bit of help. She’s feeling faint.”
Charlotte’s eyes gleamed with anticipation. “Of course, Rose. I’ll make sure she’s well taken care of.” As Rose passed by Charlotte, she leaned in close and whispered, “There’s a bag behind her chair; it contains things you may find useful.” Something about the gleam in Charlotte’s eyes gave Seraphina pause. She had seen that look before—just not always on the faces of survivors. With a final nod, Seraphina, as Rose, slipped quietly out of the salon, her mission complete. Once in the corridor, she donned her cape and veil, blending seamlessly back into the guise of anonymity. Her footsteps were soft and measured as she exited the hotel.
Outside, the evening air was cool against her skin. She spotted a runner boy loitering nearby, his cap askew and eyes alert for work.
“Here, lad,” Rose—now fully Seraphina—called softly, handing him a coin and a sealed note. “Deliver this to Felix Dunsley, at the Illustrated London News. It’s urgent.”
The boy nodded, pocketing the coin with a quick smile. “Right away, ma’am!” he chirped before darting off into the night.
Inside the hotel, Charlotte steeled herself, determination mingling with anticipation. She approached Mrs. Blackthorn, who sat, lulled by the laudanum, in the plush chair.
“Mrs. Blackthorn,” Charlotte began, her voice low and firm. “Allow me to assist you.”
Mrs. Blackthorn blinked slowly, her mind clouded. “Charlotte, dear? What are you—”
But Charlotte silenced her with a glance, retrieving the bag Rose had mentioned. Inside, she found ropes, gloves, and other items—tools for enacting her long-held revenge.
By the time Felix Dunsley arrived at the Langham Hotel, the atmosphere was charged with unspoken tension. He made his way to the green salon on the second floor, curiosity piqued by Seraphina’s cryptic message.
The scene that greeted him was shocking. The air was thick with the scent of scandal, and before him, Rear Admiral Hargreaves’ daughter and Mrs. Blackthorn were entwined in a lurid tableau of sapphic depravity.
The scene that met Dunsley was startling, even for a man accustomed to society’s shadows. The room smelled of perfume, laudanum, and something more intimate. Mrs. Blackthorn and Charlotte Hargreaves lay tangled together on the narrow bed, bound in a pose so charged with implication it needed no explanation. Silken cords secured Charlotte’s ankles to the bedposts, her wrists fastened behind her with padded cuffs. Her body was bare, her skin flushed and marked by signs of intense, prolonged contact.
Mrs. Blackthorn, stripped of her usual corset and dignity, lay collapsed across Charlotte. A medical device—an electrical stimulator commonly prescribed for hysteria—hummed quietly on the bed beside them, its wires trailing across the floor. Between them, a leather harness with an attached two-way godemiche hinted at the nature of their contact, its polished fittings slick with use. A faint smile lingered on Charlotte’s lips, her expression peaceful, almost triumphant. Mrs. Blackthorn’s head rested on her chest, her powdered hair tousled, her lipstick smudged in a way that left little doubt about what had transpired.
Dunsley, steady in hand but racing in thought, surveyed the scene. He knew exactly what he was seeing: the collapse of a carefully guarded reputation, the exposure of a woman who had built her fortune on modesty, decorum, and control. He would not need to embellish. The facts alone would ruin her.
The scandal broke with a force that tore through polite society like a blade through silk. The Illustrated London News stopped just short of naming names, but other broadsheets were not so cautious. Rumors gave way to certainty, and soon every drawing room from Belgravia to Mayfair echoed with the same tale: Mrs. Blackthorn, proprietress of the Loch Thorne School for the Refinement of Wayward Ladies, had been found in the most shocking circumstances imaginable—with one of her own charges, no less. The names, the details, the illustrations—each more damning than the last—left no room for denial.
Mrs. Blackthorn did not face trial. Her friends abandoned her. Her staff disappeared. What remained of her wealth was quietly redirected to ensure a scandal of this scale did not touch more prominent names. And so, within days, she was removed from public view entirely. Doctors, summoned by her remaining family, pronounced her unfit—morally compromised and dangerously excitable. She was committed to the Bethlem Royal Hospital, known by another name on the street: Bedlam.
There, she was subjected to the very therapies she once recommended for others. Hydrotherapy. Restraint. Dietary controls. Weeks passed without real clothing. Months went by without conversation. Her hair was cut. Her corsets removed. She was bathed, examined, penned, and catalogued. No one came to visit. No one asked after her. She had once ruled over silence, obedience, and control. Now she sat mute in a locked room while attendants charted her moods and dosed her with mercury chloride.
With her revenge complete, Seraphina found herself at a crossroads. She had achieved what she set out to do, yet the victory felt strangely hollow. The restrictive attire she wore remained a constant companion—her tightly laced corsets, towering heels, gloves, and veils were no longer tools of reform but habits embedded deep into her daily life. Much of her inheritance had been consumed in the pursuit of justice. Now, with her enemies disgraced and gone, she faced the far more mundane question of survival.
Meanwhile, the Loch Thorne Reformatory, left leaderless in the wake of scandal, stood in quiet disarray.
Loch Thorne# Seraphina sat by the window of her London hotel, watching the soft drizzle trail down the glass. The scandal had broken precisely as intended. Mrs. Blackthorn was finished—her name spoken only in hushed, scandalized tones. The reformatory, leaderless and disgraced, had gone into quiet chaos. Girls were being sent home or relocated, instructors dismissed, and the remaining staff unsure what came next.
It was the perfect opening.
Seraphina had not been named, implicated, or even mentioned in the aftermath. She was still seen as a respectable widow of impeccable bearing, a former alumna who had emerged from Mrs. Blackthorn’s care as a model of composure and restraint. But she was also nearly out of funds. Her revenge had cost her dearly—bribes, travel, layers of disguise, and the upkeep of her appearance. She needed not only shelter and security but a future.
And perhaps, more than that, she felt something stir beneath the satisfaction of revenge: the understanding that no one else would protect those girls. Not from people like Mrs. Blackthorn. Not from the men who funded the institution and demanded obedience in exchange for charity. If someone with insight, and memory, and control did not take the reins, then another woman like Blackthorn would rise in her place.
So she drafted a letter.
It was written on pale blue stationery, the handwriting elegant and steady. It was addressed jointly to Rear Admiral Hargreaves and Lord Everingham—both discreetly involved in the reformatory’s governance. She presented herself not as a petitioner but as a solution: an alumna with firsthand understanding of what made the institution effective, but also what had allowed its failures. She proposed a new model—one that retained discipline but offered dignity. Modern restraint, gentler methods, and outcomes that would appeal to both society and the press.
She emphasized her neutrality in the scandal, her respectability, and her knowledge of the girls’ needs—emotional, behavioral, and educational. She positioned herself not as a reformer, but as someone who could protect the reformatory from further scrutiny by quietly restoring its purpose under new, careful leadership.
Both men replied within the week. A luncheon was arranged. At the table, she spoke with warmth, precision, and a hint of humility. She acknowledged the difficulties ahead, but assured them she had the discretion and steadiness to lead. Lord Everingham, ever pragmatic, admired her composure. Rear Admiral Hargreaves, perhaps remembering his daughter’s troubled path, respected her poise.
Within a fortnight, a formal announcement was made—quietly, without press or notice.
Mrs. Seraphina Arabella Hartwell was appointed Headmistress of the Loch Thorne School for the Refinement of Wayward Ladies.
Soon after assuming her new role as Headmistress, Seraphina began to sense the difference between managing a vision and enforcing one. Most of the girls at Loch Thorne adapted quickly to the restructured routines—softer in tone than Mrs. Blackthorn’s, but no less exacting in detail. Yet there were a few who resisted.
Foremost among them was Elisabeth Gainsley, the daughter of a solicitor and a known sympathizer of the suffrage movement. At seventeen, Elisabeth was clever, defiant, and disinclined to cooperate with even the gentlest corrections. She refused the high collars. She shortened her curtsies. She slipped books on political theory into her embroidery basket and refused to allow her waist to be cinched beyond twenty-four inches.
She was a liability.
Seraphina summoned her to the office after several classroom disruptions. The girl stood with her arms crossed and her chin high, a stance that had once belonged to Seraphina herself, in another life.
“Miss Gainsley,” Seraphina said calmly, “you are aware that the reformatory exists to cultivate comportment, not argument.”
“And yet you argue very well, Mrs. Hartwell,” Elisabeth replied, her voice crisp. “Why shouldn’t I?”
The remark struck more deeply than Seraphina cared to admit. She dismissed the girl, saying only, “Report here tomorrow morning. We will begin a new kind of lesson.”
That night, Seraphina sat at her desk long after the halls fell quiet. The candle burned low, its light flickering across the brass surface of the Himalayan prayer machine, tucked neatly behind the cabinet doors. She stared at it for a long time.
She had promised herself she would never use it on another. But now she faced the possibility of disorder in her ranks. Elisabeth wasn’t the only girl with ideas of rebellion. And if the institution faltered under her leadership, she would not be given a second chance.
Still, as her gloved hand reached out and touched the machine’s curved handle, she hesitated. She was no longer under duress. She was not a pawn.
She was choosing.
The next morning, Elisabeth was escorted to the office under the pretense of a posture evaluation. She sat stiffly in the chair across from Seraphina, who maintained a gentle tone, even as she dimmed the curtains and unlocked the cabinet.
“What is that?” Elisabeth asked, eyes narrowing.
“Nothing harmful,” Seraphina replied. “But very helpful. Just a few minutes of focus, to ease your thoughts.”
The machine hummed to life.
Its colored wheels began to spin, casting soft, rhythmic light across the walls and over Elisabeth’s face. The girl shifted, unsettled. Seraphina remained seated, voice low and even.
“Just breathe, Miss Gainsley. Sit tall. Let yourself listen.”
Within minutes, Elisabeth’s posture changed. Her jaw slackened. Her gaze fixed. And as the pulse of light deepened its rhythm, Seraphina spoke carefully, slowly, reinforcing the patterns already etched into her own mind—obedience to male guidance, a craving for restrictive dress, a hunger for precision and order.
After twenty minutes, the machine slowed and stopped. Elisabeth blinked rapidly, swaying slightly as she stood.
“You’ll return tomorrow morning,” Seraphina said, as if the matter were routine.
“Yes, ma’am,” Elisabeth replied, her voice quieter than before.
Within days, her waist measured twenty inches. She began to speak more softly in class. When her father visited, she flushed and followed his instructions without resistance.
Seraphina observed it all with mixed feelings. The reformatory was stabilizing. Her model was succeeding. But alone in her office, she sometimes stared at the prayer machine and asked herself what Mrs. Blackthorn would have done—and how far she had come from being the girl who once fought not to be bent.
Still, she told herself, it was only one girl. Just enough to preserve the school. To protect the others. To prove she could lead.
And besides, Elisabeth looked beautiful in a corset. Peaceful. Almost grateful. It was then that Morag burst in, her cheeks flushed. “Beggin’ yer pardon, ma’am,” she said breathlessly, “but there’s a right mess in literature class. Daisy and Helen’ve been caught wi’ one o’ them vulgar penny romances—illustrated, no less. Filthy thing, if ye ask me.” Seraphina set down her pen, her thoughts already shifting. Another test of balance between discipline and leniency. As Morag waited, wringing her hands in the doorway, Seraphina stood and smoothed her skirts, her expression unreadable. “Bring them to my office,” she said calmly. “We’ll settle this before luncheon.”
Loch Thorne, Autumn 1985# The wind off the water hit harder than she’d expected.
Claire Alden stood at the edge of the narrow dock, her canvas duffel slung over one shoulder, jacket zipped to the chin. The Loch stretched before her like a piece of cut slate, dull and silver, reflecting nothing. Across the water sat the island, dense with pine and mist, and on its rise—half-choked in bracken and shadow—stood the building. The reformatory.
She hadn’t even known she had Scottish roots until the lawyer called. Something about a great-aunt several times removed. A reclusive widow. A name scratched into a will no one remembered drafting. Now, after three plane rides, two train transfers, a hired car, and one very narrow road full of sheep and fog, she was here. At the edge of her inheritance.
She still wasn’t sure what she’d inherited, exactly. When the solicitor mentioned “a mansion,” Claire had imagined something modest, maybe ivy-covered stone and a few creaking rooms. Not an island. Not that hulking silhouette rising through the mist like a fortress abandoned mid-siege. She hadn’t even known she had Scottish ancestry—no stories, no tartan, nothing passed down. Just this. Some great-aunt with a widow’s name and no known heirs, and now Claire, staring at the edge of her own family’s ghost story. She figured she’d stay a day or two, take a look around, maybe get a sense of the place. Then what? Sell it, probably. Unless it couldn’t be sold. Unless it wasn’t worth anything at all.
“Right then,” the woman beside her said. “Let’s not dawdle.”
The ferry was barely more than a boat—dark green, metal-hulled, and dented in places that suggested age and experience, like its owner.
The ferryman—ferrywoman—was named Isla Duncan. A stout woman in a thick wool sweater, with hair tied in a kerchief and boots that looked war-tested. She didn’t smile, but she wasn’t unkind.
Claire climbed aboard and sat on the metal bench as Isla pushed off with a practiced kick and turned the outboard motor. The boat trembled, then groaned forward into the water.
“Bit late in the year for sightseeing,” Isla called over the wind, voice thick with a Highland burr. “You’re the American, then?”
“I am. Claire Alden.” She offered a hand, then laughed at herself—too far to shake.
Isla nodded. “Aye, they said you’d come. Lawyer phoned MacCallum’s shop for the number. Told him I knew the way well enough.”
The wind picked up, whipping strands of Claire’s hair into her eyes. “So—what do you know about the place?”
Isla’s eyes didn’t leave the dark shape of the island. “Locals call it the Hartwell House, but that’s not what it was, not really. It was a school. Or… a kind of school. For girls. They called it a reformatory back then. Victorian times. Girls sent there to learn their place, if you catch the meaning.”
Claire raised an eyebrow. “That sounds ominous.”
“Aye. Was,” Isla said. “The women ran it—strict types. Real lace-and-discipline sort. They say the headmistress came from the colonies, India maybe, wore black every day and never once unlaced her corset. Mad as a hatter, but elegant, so they say. Mrs. Hartwell, she was called. No one saw her much in town, but the ferrymen used to bring crates for her—cases of gloves, veils, corsets, and dresses tailored too tightly for comfort. Things too fine for island living. Things meant for display, or for correction. She ran the place like a queen. Girls came off the island changed, if they came back at all.”
Claire felt a chill that had nothing to do with the weather.
“So what happened to it?”
Isla shifted in her seat, frowning. “Closed just before the war. Some say the government got interested. Some say there was a scandal. Most just say it got too strange. Last few girls weren’t right, they say. Always quiet. Posture too good. Wouldn’t speak unless spoken to.”
The island loomed larger now, its trees rising dark and still behind the broken stone wall that rimmed the landing cove.
“Weren’t any family left, not that we knew,” Isla continued. “But I suppose you’re it now. The Hartwell line, or some long thread of it.”
Claire managed a laugh, thin as the wind. “Not a name I’ve ever heard in my family.”
“No surprise. Families bury the strange ones. Easier to forget.”
The boat slowed as they reached the landing—a short bridge of warped wood lashed to rusting moorings. A wrought-iron lantern hung askew from a post, its glass cloudy with age. The steps leading to the path had recently been scraped clean of moss. Beyond the landing, the gravel path curved up into the trees toward the house, which loomed in partial view beyond the rise.
Claire climbed out, her boots thudding against the damp planks. The trees whispered faintly now, wind curling through the pines. But there was no carriage. No figures waiting at the gate. Just the iron arch above the gravel path, its sign still faintly legible in the twilight.
Just the silence of abandonment.
Isla remained in the boat a moment longer, then reached under the bench for two crates. “Right—provisions,” she said, hauling them onto the dock. “Bit of bread, tea, tinned soup," she tapped one crate. “Greens, potatoes, and a bit of meat,” she tapped the other. “Not fancy, but enough for a few days.” She set the crates down near the steps. “Fuel was brought over three days back, and we tested the generators and boiler then. Still working, if a bit temperamental. Just don’t rush them.”
Claire nodded, taking the sack from her. “That’s… nice, now that it’s getting colder.”
Isla shrugged. “Folk in town don’t much talk about this place, but we don’t forget it, either. And MacCallum doesn’t like an inheritance gone cold.”
Claire turned to look at the building. The reformatory stood two stories tall, all blackened stone and arched windows—many boarded, others bare like staring eyes. Ivy had crept up the sides and died there, brittle against the stone. The roof sloped steep and narrow, chimney stacks rising like sentries. The front door sat beneath a half-circle portico of cracked columns. A brass plate on the lintel read:
“Loch Thorne School for the Refinement of Wayward Ladies”
The lettering was worn but legible.
Claire exhaled, long and slow. “This is it?”
Isla nodded. “Aye. Might not look it now, but she was once a grand place. Strange. Beautiful. And full of rules.” She paused. “You planning to stay long?”
Claire looked up at the windows again. “A few days. Just long enough to figure out what I’ve inherited.”
Isla gave a wry smile. “That’s the trick, isn’t it? Knowing what you’ve inherited. I’ll check in day after tomorrow.”
And with that, the ferry engine growled to life, and Isla Duncan began to pull away from the dock, her silhouette shrinking against the slate-gray mist. Claire stood at the edge of the dock until the boat faded into the fog, the hum of its engine swallowed by distance.
Then she turned toward the house. She was alone. The house watched.
Lugging the crates was harder than she’d expected. The path to the house climbed gently but steadily, and the wind bit at her as she made the slow trudge uphill, stopping every dozen steps to shift the weight. Her jacket was damp with sweat by the time she reached the porch.
The keys waited beneath the porch stone. They were easy to find—cold and heavy in Claire’s hand, the old brass loop clinking softly as she lifted the slab and found them just where Isla had said they’d be.
She caught her breath, bent double for a moment, then stood and turned the key in the lock. The front door creaked open with effort, the hinges groaning like something roused from sleep.
Inside, the air was dry and heavy with dust. Not decay, exactly—just stillness. The kind of stillness that settles in a place long waiting to be remembered.
She set her bag down in the vestibule and took a moment to breathe it in. Cold. Sharp. But not damp. The floors were wood, dark with age, still gleaming in places where varnish had held on. Oil lamps were mounted on the walls beside electric sconces, a strange overlap of eras. Wires traced along the moldings toward switches that looked pre-war, at best.
Claire lugged the crates inside and, for now, stored them just behind the entry doors.
She descended to the basement first, guided by a narrow staircase and the faint metallic scent of machinery. The air there was colder, but not unbearable. A small metal door yielded to the turn of a key, and beyond it: the generators.
Claire whistled. “Well, you’re not what I expected.”
The equipment was well-maintained, surprisingly modern—1950s, maybe early ’60s. Clean lines. Industrial beige. She found the control panel, flipped a few switches, and the generators hummed to life without protest. A moment later, overhead bulbs buzzed on. Not all, but enough to scatter the shadows. MacCallum had done fine work, keeping things oiled and fueled.
She found the boiler next—oil-fed, hulking, squat. A flip of another switch, a mechanical cough, and then warmth, low and growing.
She stood in the glow for a long moment, arms wrapped around herself. A place this size would need a great deal of heating to be comfortable. But something told her comfort had never been the priority for the girls who lived here.
Upstairs again, light chased away the gloom as she explored the building. She found the kitchen and put her supplies in there for later.
The building had been used as a boarding school. The first hall stretched long, lined with narrow doors. She opened one, then another. Thick oakwood, more solid than necessary. The bedrooms—if they could be called that—were spartan cells, with high window slits letting in weak light. But the beds were carved and solid, with pressed linens still folded at the foot. Each room had a dressing stand, a mirror, a small wooden chest. Personal. But in the way of a monastery. Or a convent. Or a prison.
The classrooms came next—larger rooms with blackboards still mounted, desks bolted to the floor in perfect, straight rows. Pre-war furniture: ink wells, carved initials, iron hooks for satchels. One desk still had a book inside.
An Introduction to Domestic Order and Feminine Resolve.
Claire snorted, but didn’t move on just yet. She flipped the book open, thumbing through brittle pages filled with neat handwriting, diagrams of posture, meal plans, even instructions for lacing corsets to precise measurements. Her brow furrowed. This wasn’t just outdated—it was disturbing.
She let the book fall shut with a soft thump. “Jesus,” she muttered, her voice echoing faintly off the chalk-dusted walls. “What the hell kind of place was this?”
She looked around again, slower this time, the weight of inheritance settling heavier on her shoulders. Not a house. Not even a school. A system, built to mold girls into someone else’s idea of right. And now it was hers.
She continued down the hall and came to a room labeled “Fitting Room” in faded gilt script.
Inside, floor-to-ceiling cupboards lined the walls. She opened one and found rows of neatly hung uniforms. Identical sets in all sizes: coarse slips, drab gray corsets, narrow underskirts, and charcoal wool dresses so stiff and scratchy they looked like they could stand on their own. Each uniform came with a pair of woolen stockings, black high-heeled boots, kid gloves, detachable stiff white collars, plain aprons, and bonnets. Everything was labeled, catalogued, preserved.
On the far wall, a framed illustration depicted the proper way to wear the uniform. A girl stood stiffly, chin tucked, gloved hands folded. Next to it, another frame displayed a list of rules in formal Victorian script:
Proper, clean, and complete uniform at all times
Always speak with decorum: “Ma’am” and “Sir” only
Curtsies before and after speaking
No speaking unless addressed
Eyes downcast unless responding
Claire stepped back, studying it. The illustration. The rules. The implication.
She turned to the uniforms again, running a hand down the boning of a corset.
“They really wore this every day?” she muttered.
There was a strange pull to it—fascination mixed with discomfort. Part of her wanted to know what it felt like. Not out of nostalgia, but curiosity. Just to understand what had been expected. She checked a few labels—yes, they’d have her size. It would be easy enough to try one on.
But she didn’t. Not yet. This wasn’t dress-up. These weren’t costumes. Whatever this place had been, it took itself seriously. And it had taken its girls even more seriously.
Claire closed the cupboard gently and stepped back into the corridor, the overhead lights flickering as if deciding whether to stay on.
Then she found it.
At the end of the west wing, behind a pair of heavy doors that stuck in their frame, lay a room unlike the others. Tall-ceilinged. Almost bare. The air was warmer, filled with golden late afternoon light that poured through an enormous arched window. And in the center of the room, on a large carved table, stood a box catching the sun.
She turned to the table itself—a broad slab of carved wood, its surface cleared for the box, but with several drawers beneath.
One stuck slightly, then gave. Inside lay a thick ledger, leather-bound, its edges gilded and worn with use. The cover bore no title—just a single embossed monogram: S.H.
Claire lifted it out, blowing dust from the top.
Inside: names. Lines and lines of entries in tidy script, columns dated between 1901 and 1935.
Pupil Name. Parent or Guardian. Cause for Admission. Tier of Treatment. Annual Fee. Outcome.
She skimmed:
“Beatrice Weatherby – Col. Weatherby (ret.) – Improper correspondence with stablehand – Advanced Therapy – £700 – Married, 1912 (Brig. Saunders, 1st Lancers)”
“Diana Fortescue – Lady Fortescue – “Strong-mindedness,” refusal to wear proper dress – Advanced Therapy – £700 – Married, 1914 (A. Calthorpe, solicitor)”
“Eleanor Macintyre – Mrs. J. Macintyre – Disobedience, chronic lateness, academic pride – Standard Instruction – £100 – Emigrated to Canada, 1925”
Claire turned quickly through the pages. There were dozens more. Maybe hundreds.
The handwriting changed after 1919, but the pattern didn’t. Always the same: cause, fee, outcome. “Advanced Therapy” appeared in bold, with extra ticks and occasional notes in the margin.
“Mild resistance in months 2–5. Breakthrough after corset regimen intensified. Full compliance observed by 8th month. Advanced therapy recommended bimonthly thereafter.”
Claire’s pulse quickened. “Advanced therapy? What the hell was that?” Claire stared at the pages, the tidy handwriting suddenly grotesque. These weren’t just school records. They were product sheets. Girls sent in, behavior cited, price paid, and outcome—always marriage, always to someone who wanted a wife shaped just so. It read like livestock entries. As if “strong-mindedness” were an illness. As if “full compliance” were a goal. Her stomach turned.
This wasn’t a school. It was a factory. And “Advanced Therapy” wasn’t education—it was correction. Reform, maybe. Or erasure.
She looked around the room again, newly unsettled by the silence, by the neatness. Whoever ran this place had done so with purpose. And someone—several someones—had paid for it. Encouraged it. Expected it. Handed over their daughters who did not conform to the standards their families demanded, reshaped into model women fit for marriage, society, or silence.
Claire exhaled slowly, the air thick in her lungs. She closed the ledger gently, as if shutting the book might muffle what she’d just learned. It didn’t.
A second book in that drawer was obviously a diary. She flipped forward, past faded ink, until she came to a marked entry near the middle.
August 17th, 1899
Today marks the final settlement of accounts with the Hargreaves estate. With the Rear Admiral’s passing and no male heir to contest, I have at last secured full ownership of the institution. Lord Everingham proved gracious, as ever—his patronage remains vital, but he sees the wisdom in unified leadership. A school cannot thrive by committee. Continuity has been preserved. I have written to the solicitor confirming the dissolution of the founding consortium. I hold the deeds myself now. The reformatory’s future is mine to shape, without compromise, without interference.
May it remain a place of discipline and order in an era increasingly given over to indulgence. I shall carry forward its mission—refined, yes, but unswerving.
Claire frowned. She flipped to the front, toward the earliest entries, and read.
January 2nd, 1885 It is not without some heaviness of heart that I accept the burden placed upon me today. The reformatory was never my ambition, nor do I imagine myself a natural schoolmistress. But with my husband’s affairs concluded, and my situation pressing as it is, I cannot afford discretion. And yet I do not despair.
With Mrs. Blackthorn’s… departure—at last—and with her, I pray, the cruelty she so thinly veiled as correction. I will run the school differently. Not softly, but justly. The girls must be guided, not broken. Restrained, but not humiliated. There is dignity in discipline if meted with compassion.
This place can change them for the better, I am sure of it. It need only change its heart first.
Claire closed the book.
It didn’t add up. That first voice—tentative, almost tender—was a world away from the cold precision of the ledger. Somewhere between that winter and the turn of the century, Mrs. Hartwell had changed. Or the school had. Or both.
And whatever “Advanced Therapy” was, it hadn’t been born of compassion. Claire needed to understand what had truly happened in this place.
Her gaze drifted back to the box.
It didn’t belong here. Not in a Victorian stone mansion tucked away in the Scottish highlands. The box was made of dark, polished wood—almost black, with a lacquered sheen—and carved all over in intricate, swirling patterns that shimmered faintly when the light hit them. Not floral. Not quite geometric. Almost… alive. The corners were inlaid with what looked like jade, cool and green, while the panels shimmered with embedded stones: turquoise, lapis, violet glass, flakes of gold. Delicate scrolls and cylinders were integrated into the design, like a music box crossed with something religious. The whole thing radiated presence. Not just exotic—ritualistic. As if it had come from somewhere older, deeper, and far from here.
Claire stepped forward, holding her breath, and laid both hands on the lid. It opened like a triptych. The outer panels folded back with a soft click, revealing a strange, layered interior: brass rods, interlocked gears, scrollwork spindles, and etched plates that caught the sunlight like fire.
She had no idea what it was.
But she was certain it had been used. Many times.
She turned one of the cylinders. It moved with a gentle resistance, then clicked into place.
A hum began. Low and deep. It settled into her chest like distant thunder rolling through stone. Behind the embedded gems, lights began to stir—faint at first, then brightening into a full cascade of motion and color. Sapphire, emerald, violet, gold—reflections spun across the walls and floor like living prisms gone wild.
Claire watched.
She meant to look away. She even tried, just for a second. To laugh. To mutter “What the hell is this thing?” But she didn’t. The lights pulsed in slow rhythm, each wave of color drawing her deeper inward. The hum settled into her bones. Her breath slowed.
Her shoulders lowered.
The buzz of thought began to fade, smoothed into stillness. Behind her eyes, the tightness unwound.
She sat down without thinking—on the edge of a trunk, or maybe a stool—her gaze still locked on the machine. It moved in delicate motion now, cylinders turning, light shifting in time. She couldn’t look away. Didn’t want to.
Time stuttered, then vanished.
The light seemed to fill the space where thought had been. Her limbs were heavy. Her mind, warm. The outside world dulled into quiet.
She blinked once.
The machine continued. The lights shimmered. The hum vibrated low and sweet.
She didn’t move.
And then—softly, like a thought not quite hers—came a voice beneath the hum, a whisper inside the stillness:
You don’t have to think right now. Just listen.

Introduction# Sonia: Meet Lass-Vash-2024# Subject: Meet Lass-Vash-2024: A Plot Twist in Viral Evolution?
Hey Anna,
Hope this finds you well and not too buried in your latest genomic conquests. I came across something bizarre and immediately thought, “This is a job for Anna’s superpowers!” So, here’s the scoop on the latest viral diva making waves: the Large Self-Stabilizing Viral Airborne Shenzhen Strain, or as I’ve affectionately dubbed it, Lass-Vash-2024.
This little monster is sporting a genome so massive it’s like it’s trying to compensate for something. We’re talking way beyond the usual viral bling, and into the territory of “Are you sure you’re not a misplaced eukaryote?” Its genomic sequence is a sprawling metropolis, and tucked within its concrete jungle are genes that act like meticulous city planners, ensuring replication fidelity is top-notch. Basically, it’s got its own internal QA team running 24/7 checks to avoid typos in its genetic manuscript.
Now, for the weird part (because, of course, there had to be one): despite its genetic overkill, Lass-Vash-2024 seems to fancy itself as a dramatist rather than a doomsday device. The symptoms are straight out of a B-rated sci-fi–think a nasty three-day cold meets a horror movie marathon, complete with headaches, vomiting, and, get this, vividly bad dreams. It’s like our viral friend is moonlighting as a mediocre dream director.
The disproportionality of it all is baffling. With such a complex genome, you’d expect it to be plotting world domination, not sending people on guilt trips for eating the last cookie in their dreams. It’s like bringing a quantum computer to a tic-tac-toe game.
I’ve got a hunch there’s more to this story, and who better to unravel this genomic Gordian knot than you? How about we tag-team this? A bit of “Anna and Sonia’s Excellent Adventure: Pandemic Edition?” We could use some of your sequencing magic to dig deeper. Maybe it’s hiding something revolutionary in its overly ambitious genetic script.
Let’s chat more over coffee? My treat–and I promise to keep the dream talk to a minimum. Say, your favorite café by the lake, this Saturday?
Stay awesome and uninfected,
Sonia

Absolutely thrilled (and a tad terrified) about our new viral star, Lass-Vash-2024. Your description had me at “genomic overkill.” Count me in for a deep dive into its genetic labyrinth – sounds like the kind of challenge that gets my sequencers humming.

Best,
Anna
Sonia: Maylee Shufoo’s Closet of Wonders and Woes# Subject: Fashion Finds: Maylee Shufoo’s Closet of Wonders and Woes
Hey Anna,
You won’t believe the fashion odyssey I’ve stumbled upon here in Shenzhen. Picture this: a boutique chain named Maylee Shufoo (美丽束缚) that’s essentially what you’d get if a Victorian-era tailor, a modern office fashion designer, and a bondage gear creator decided to collaborate. Yes, it’s as bizarre and fascinating as it sounds.
First off, the pencil skirts here redefine “restrictive”–imagine trying to navigate a lab in one of those. I reckon I’d need a couple of those gene-splicing skills just to make it to the coffee machine without toppling over. And the heels–oh, the heels! They’re skyscrapers! I’m half-convinced they’re designed for people who’ve evolved past the need for feet.
Then there are the corsets, available with or without shoulder braces, because why not add a dash of posture correction to your daily fashion? It’s like saying, “I’m not only breathlessly chic, but I’m also literally breathless.”
Photo Attachment: Inside Maylee Shufoo’s in Shenzhen.
And let’s not even start on the blouses–buttoned at the back, with a collar tight enough to ensure you remember every decision that led you to wear it. They are complemented by long gloves adorned with an absurd number of minuscule buttons. It’s like they were designed for someone with the patience of a saint and the dexterity of a surgeon.
The mix of aesthetics is wild – there’s an air of office chic meets Victorian discipline meets a splash of traditional Chinese elegance. All tied up with a hint of “I might need a safe word to get out of this outfit.” It’s a peculiar style-mix that somehow works here,
or at least, attracts enough attention to sustain a chain of stores.
I can almost hear your laughter from here, imagining the look on your face as you try to picture me navigating my way through the boutique, doing my best not to look completely out of my element. I promise to bring back photos, and maybe a souvenir or two–though I might skip the corset. The last thing I need is an impromptu lesson in Victorian fainting techniques.
Looking forward to our coffee chat and your thoughts on whether genomics can explain why someone would design a blouse that requires an assistant to put on.
Stay fabulous and free-moving,
Sonia
Anna: Re: Maylee Shufoo’s Closet of Wonders and Woes# Subject: Re: Fashion Finds: Maylee Shufoo’s Closet of Wonders and Woes

“50 Shades of Shenzhen Chic,” huh? Should I be concerned about these newfound hobbies of yours, or is this purely for “research” purposes? 🤔😂 I’m kind of expecting you to return with a PhD in Fashion Restraint Dynamics at this rate.
Seriously though, a photo or, dare I say, a haul video? Now, that would be priceless! On a more serious note, safe travels back, and make sure you’re not too jet-lagged for our coffee catch-up. And remember, no corsets on the flight back; we wouldn’t want you to pass out somewhere over Siberia.

Anna

title: Dressing Sonia (from the World of 'Infection')
